AUCTIONING OFF THE BABY. What am I offered for Baby? Dainty, dimpled, and sweet From the curls above his forehead To the beautiful rosy feet, From the tips of the wee pink fingers To the light of the clear brown eye, What am I offered for Baby? Who'll buy? Who'll buy? Who'll buy? What am I offered for Baby? "A shopful of sweets ?" Ah, no! That's too much beneath his value Who is sweetest of all below I• The naughty, beautiful darling One kiss from his rosy mouth Is better than all the dainties Of East or West or South ! What am I offered for Baby? "A pile of gold ?" Ah, clear, Tour gold is too hard and bears, To purch=e my brightness here. Would the treasures of all the mountains, -.. Far in the wonderful lands, Be worth the clinging and clasping Of these dear little peach-bloom handsf So whatam I offered for Baby? "A rape of diamonds?" Nay, ' if your brilliants were larger and brighter Than stars in the Milky Way, Would they ever be half so precious As'the light of those lustrous eyes, ,Still ull of the heavenly glory They brought from behind the skies. Then whet am I offered for Baby ? " A heart full of love and a kiss. Well, if anything ever could tempt me 'Tivould be such an offer as this! :Eat how can I know if your loving Is tender and true and divine, • Enough to repay what I'm giving In selling this sweetheart of mine? So we will not sell the Baby! Your gold and gems and stuff Were they ever so rare and precious Would never be half enough! For what would we care, my dearie, What glory the world put on, If our beautiful darling were going, If our beautiful darling were gone. Mercury 'Supplement.

A LAY OF CIVILISATION. A train spZ,d on a road banked o'er the lanes And courts ignoble of our monstrous Fast; Wherefrom glad children laden with spring flowers Fluttered white kerchiefs cheering. At a window Of one of those poor dwellings a pale child Waved his lean arm responsive; his hurrah Was drowned in theirs; .they saw not the wan smile Of thateven-year-old cripple; in a cot, That seemed an orange-case disused, he lay, Propped high for him to see the bright live trains Rush past with human freight. An ancient dame Tended the child, his grandmother; they two Lived ever here; the boy knew no green fields; Through the long days, and late into the nights, (When her frail charge lay peacefully in sleep, And when to wakeful voyagers by rail The shadow of the love-invented cot On the illumined blind appeared to be 7 That of a little coffin; ah ! great Love! Wilt thou soon lay the lad in such a cot?) The old woman plied her scissors and her needle For a poor pittance; one rich offering Of sweet burned incense, all her selfless soul Is offered up to Heaven for the child. 'I he dame hath taught her helpless one to road, Buying him Noah's ark and picture-book, And she hath helped him order on the floor A mimic park with turfs from a lark's cage, Wherein are planted perpendicular Thin sticks of deal, their foliage woolly shreds From old frayed borders of the grandame's gown; A baking-dish contains the mimic lake, And, swimming there, a dinted bird, once whito. These are unbeautiful; the neighbouring scene Affronts our every sense; Plague, Famine lurk With heads obscene, with sly lack-lustre eyes, Couching at every threshold motionless. Yet here, yea, here, not where the lark pours joy, Evermore pouring ecstasies in air .Of rapturous blue, nor where a throstle wafts His incense of clear notes upon the.breeae, O'erquavered by soft shadows of young leaves; Nor where, with age-long rapture, holy men Dream swooning visions in Himalayan snows— Not there, but here I find me at Heaven's gate, Open to let the t te:nal Sun shine through On our sad Earth; fair angels come nudge In this poor hovea, for Queen Love lives here., With dear handmaidens, Patienee, Tenderness, And her fair a-arr:or-knight, young Fortitude. —Front "Sonys of the Heiglds and Defy!'

Every day is a little life, and our whole life is but a etay repeated. Therefore, live as if it would be the last. The world was sad—the garden was a wild; And Man, the hermit, sighed—till Woman smiled. A loving heart arid a pleasant countenance are com- modities which a man should .never fail to take home with him. Does yore kape 110 thin' but dry goods hero ?" "No, ma'am." Al Thin where will Ibe afther goin' for a watered silk?" Good temper. like a sunny day, sheds a brightness over everything. It is the sweetener of toil and the soother of disquietude.--Ireing. St. Thomas A Aquinas from his earliest childhood felt the greatest repugnance to applause, so that a word in his own praise was never let to escape from his lips. "Did you pass the hat ?" the pastor of a Texas con- gregation asked the deacon after the morning service. "Yes; I did.," said the deacon, and then looking into the vlcAnt interior of a hat that had nothing but lining, he added, gloomily, "So did everybody else." " G'mawaing, Eph. What am you doin' fur a libin' dese days ?" "Me? Wy, 'sistant sup'intendent ob de biges' railroad in dis country." " Glong ! Yon doan' told me! Golly, Eph ! What does de 'sistant sup'inten- den' have to do?" "Nuthin' but 'sist the sup'intenden' when he wants to pat on his obercoat an' sieh: An American minister forgot to take his sermon with him to church, and his wife discovering the mistake, sent it to him in charge of a small boy, who was to re- ceive ten cents for the job. Presently he returned for the mosey. "You delivered the sermon, did you ?" she asked. "No, mum," he replied. "I jest gu• it to ; be's a deliverin' of it himself." Not long ago a lady who had just returned from Europe was asked by a friend if she had seen the lion of St. Mark. 'Oh, yes !" she replied; "we just arrived in time to see the noble creature fed." The late Dr. Beadle of Philadelphia must have encountered the same lady. He spAre of the beauty of the Dardanelles, and she re- replied, "Oh, yes! I know them welL They are intimate friends of mine." _ .

The smallest-, thing can tempt. As poor John Buny.an iid o -Ice, something kept tempting him to sell Christ. If he stooped to ipelc up a pin the voice said, "Sell Him for th it! Sell Him for that !" And men sell their honour for things as cheap. A pin will do it; a sweet smile; a fair face; the ruby wine; the love of money. Ah. for what has not man sold his soul I—George Damson. Kind words are the music of the world. They have a power which seems to be beyond natural causes, as if they were some angel's song which had lost its way and come on earth, and sang on undyingly, smiting the hearts of men with sweetest wounds, and putting for the while an angelic nature in us. Hard words, on the other hand, are like hailstones in summer, beating down and destroying what they would nourish were they melted into drops...
Others -shall sing the song, Others shall right the wrong,— Finish what I begin, And all I fail of win. What matter, I or they? Mine or another's day, So the right word be said, •

And life be sweeter made 2—Whittier.; Not long since a New Hampshire committee-man was examining an infant school class. "Can any little girl or boy give the definition of the word ' average ?" he asked. For some time no one replied, but finally a little girl hesitatingly said, "It is a thing a hen lays an egg on, sir." "No, that's not right." "Yes, sir, my book says so ;" and she trotted up to her questioner and pointed to this sentence in her reading-book, "A hen lays an egg every day on an average." Our lives are songs; God writes the words, And we set them to music at pleasure; And the song grows glad, or sweet or sad, As we choose to fashion the measure. We must write the music, whatever the song, Whatever its rhyme or metre; And if it is sad, we can make it glad, Or if sweet, we can make it sweeter. A COUNTRY GIRL'S FORTUNE.—During the troubles in the reign of Charles I. a country girl is said to have come up to London in search of a place as a servant- maid; but, not succeeding, she applied herself to carry- ing out beer from a brewhouse, and was one of those then called " tub-women." The brewer, observing a well-looking girl in this low occupation, took her into his family as a servant, and, after a little while, she be- having herself with so much prudence and decorum he married her; but he died when she was yet a young woman, and left her a large fortune. The business of tile brewery was dropped, and the young woman ,was recommended to Mr. Hyde, as a gentleman of skill in the law, to settle her affairs. Hyde (who was afterwards Earl of Clarendon)., finding the widow's fortune very considerable, married her. Of this marriage there was no other issue than a daughter, who was afterwards the wife of James 11., and mother of Mary and Anne, queens of England. Life seems long at the start; it does not seem so long at the last. No greater comfort than to know much; no less labour than to say little. A week's bad example at home will undo three months' teaching at school. 1 The line of life is a ragged diagonal between duty and eeiiire.—W: 11. Alger. Let thy will be thy friend, thy mind thy companion, thy tongue thy servant. People say sometimes, "See what I have overcome; I see hew cheerful I am; see how completely I have tri- umphed over these black events.' Not if they still re- mind me of the Wack event.—Bsterson. Unselash and noble acts are the most radiant epochs in the biography of souls. When wrought in earliest youth, they lie in the memory of age like the,coral islands —green and sunny, amidst the melanclsoly waste of

ocean. A .FACT.—A short time ago, in one of our large ma- chine shop's, a man was .given a shaft to reduce 1-16th in. dia. He asked the foreman whether he should turn it off or file it off ! TEe was told to =file.himself "off," which he did. "Why don't you go to work ?" said a charitable lady the other day to a tramp, before whom she had placed a nicely cooked meal. "I would," replied the vagrant, "if I had the tools." "What sort of tools do you want?' asked his hostess. "A knife and fork." A wealthy Irish farmer' intending to "send his son to college," recently wrote a letter to "the heads of Oxford University," in which he said, "Please say what are • 'our terms for a year; and will it cost anything extra if my son learns to write a good hand and:spell proper, 'es well as to row a boat ?" An alderman once called on a well-known doctor, when the following dialogue took place :—" Doctor, I have strong tendency to'.gout ; what shall I do to arrest it ?" "Take a bucket of water and a ton of anthracite three times a week." "How ?" " Drink the former, and carry the latterup three pairs of stairs." "This is George the Fourth," said an exhibitor of wax- work for the million, at threepence each, pointing to a very slim figure, with a theatrical crown on his •head. "I thought he was a very stout man," observed a-spec- tator. "Very likely," replied the man, shortly, not approving of the comment of his visitor; "bit it:you'd been here without victuals half so long as he has you'd have been twice as thin." During a steam voyage, on a sudden stoppage el the machinery, considerable alarm took place, eb-pecially among the female passengers. "What is the matter?— what is the matter? For Heaven's sake tell me the worst!" exclaimed one, more anxious than the rest. After a short pause, a hoarse voice from the deck re- plied, "Nothing, madam, nothing; only a matter of fric- tion between the bottom of the vessel and the top of the

earth." Neither Sam nor his wife are very smart, as will be I seen by the following incident :—The other night Sam heard a noise under his bed. "There is somebody under the bed!" said Sam to his wife. "It's Fide." "No, I think it's a burglar," replied Sam. "Just reach your hand down, and if it is Fide he will lick it." The burglar —for it was one after all—overheard the conversation, and when Sam reached his hand down the burglar licked it all over very affectionately. This was entirely satis- factory, and they both went to sleep; but when they woke up the next morning there was not much left in the house that was worth carrying off. The last general election in South Ayrshire was very warmly contested, and for some weeks previous to the day of election, canvassing for votes was carried on with great spirit by both parties; so much so, indeed, that lukewarm politicians began to look upon canvassing as a most decided nuisance. While an old worthy was driving some cattle along the high road between New- milns and Galston, being afraid of the leaders of the herd turning off into a by-road, he shouted to a pedes- trian coming from the opposite direction, "Hey, mon, kep thee beasts," which was accordingly done. On coming close, the old man discovered that the pedestrian was no other than the parish minister of Galston. Rather taken aback, he ejaculated, "Man, minister, I didna ken it was you; I thocht it was ane o' thee oaavassin' bodies." "FORUM)" EPITAPH.—Here cool the ashes of Muleiber Grim, late of this parish, blacksmith. He was born in Seacoal-lane, and bred at Hammersmith; from his youth upwards he was much addicted to vices, and was often guilty of forgery; having some talents. for irony, he thereby produced many heats in his neighbourhood, which he usually increased by blowing up the cowls. Though he sometimes proved a warm friend, yet, where his interest was concerned, he made it a constant rule to strike while the iron was hot. He was the means of banging many of the innocent family of the Bells, under , the idle pretence of keeping them from jangling; and put great numbers of the Hearts of steel into the hot- test flames, merely (as he declared) to soften the ob- duracy of their tempers. At length, after passing a long life in the commission of these black actions, his fire being exhausted, and his bellows worn out, he filed off to that place where only the fervid ordeal of his own forge can be exceeded, declaring with his last puff that "man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upwards!" —ifeehanical Progress. THE 'rasa AND THIS GF.asiass—Charlotte G. O'Brien, daughter of Smith O'Brien, the Irish leader, has pub- fished a thoughtful and sensible paper on" The Emi- grant in New York," in which she points out the errors that have made the emigrant's lot a hard one, and offers some valuable suggestions. Her paper contains one pas- , sage of peculiar interest, as follows :—" It may be said I th German emigrants to the United States counter- balance the Irish. They do in wealth, in industry, in character, in ability, but not in political influence. The Germans spread themselves over the whole land. They are far richer, and often more successful than the Irish. • They are steadier, more ssber, more plodding.; but their aim is wealth, comfort, happy homes. They live more apart from the national life., they have their German , newspapers, and they speak their German tossgue inter- larde I with Americarnains. Now the Irishman is a brain particle: he gravitates to the life centres. He is oursed . with the vice of thinking ; he is too often the gifted , maniac, but withal he is the man who in every country but his own takes the lead. In the States the Irishman is on the press, in the law, ia the army, in all profes- sions—above all, in politics; he is a very powerful leaven for veal or evil in American life, and, grant the , rest of the nation were passive, the Irish-American nation is quite strong enough in any critical moment to turn the scale of war." THE BEAUX AND BELLES OF NEW GUINEA,—The Rev. W. G. Lewes, F.R.G.S., a missionary resident at Port Moresby, who probably knows more about the Papuan , race than any other man living, gave the following • amusing de,scriptien of the beaux and belles of New ' Guinea in the course of a recent lecture delivered in , msnesurne :—" The natives are by no means a forbidding ; and repulsive people. Imagine a man about sft. gin ; his body a nice brown oolour, and if he was a masher, it , would be covered with red earth and varnished with E oil; his face painted in different colours, a piece of , polished stone through his nose; his hair long and frizzy, ornamented with bird of paradise plumes and . cockatoo feathers; his teeth black or red; his ears • weighed down with huge ear ornaments; his waist com- pressed to waspish proportions, with a broad belt of bark; shell armlets on hi; arms, and dogs'-teeth necklaces , round his neck; a braast ornament of boar's tusk or peal . shell; a gaily painted waist ribbon with long streamers , in front and tohind ; anklets and kneelets of coloured • flax; a small netted bag over his shoulder and a chunan , pot in his hand; imagine all this, and you have a typical . New Guinean. The women match the men. The young . girls wear abundance of ornaments, but after marriage , very few. They are all profusely tattoed, and wear a ' coloured grass petticoat, which reaches to the knees. I Fashion was despotic in New Guinea, and all acknow- ledged her sway. Their get-up would create a sensa- tion on the block' in C,ollins-street, but the women judi- ciously left the tight-lacing to the men, didn't resort to i artificial emtraction or expansion, and had no six-but- ton gloves or high-heeled shoes." THE HUNGRY CHlNAHAN.—Sharp,unscrupulous trades- men are found among the placid, meek-faced China- men, as well as among the more highly civilised and obtrusive brethren of other nations. A correspondent gives the following illlustration of this fact. He was sitting with some brother officers of the United States ship Dash, in front of the English hotel in Batavia, Java, and was approached by a forlorn-looking Chinaman, who had a sword-cane in his hand. "Want buy ?" said ; he, bowing profoundly to the group. The others paid l no attention to him, but I, being somewhat inexperienced in the ways of the "childlike and bland,";took pity on him and asked him his price. "Six dollah," said he. Six dollars!" I exclaimed. "That is too much." " Velly fine . sword-cane. Chinaman velly hungly," ' whined he, plaintively. "Melican help hungry man allee time. Five dollah, sah ?" "No," said I. "Five dollars is too much." "Four dollah! little four dollah!" persisted the miserable-looking object. Still I was firm in my belief that I could buy a sword-cane for much less, if I really needed one, and declared that I would not pay four dollars. 'Ties dollah? Two dollah? One dollah ?" groaned the beggar. Then, as I shook my head in obedience to a stealthy wink from a lieutenant sitting near and watching the progress of the trade, the fellow began to cry, "No catchee chow-chow two, tlee day! Velly hungly! Die! No catchee chow-chow, die! Fifty cents?" I relented and agreed to buy it for fifty cents. But an investigation of my purse showed nothing but a ten dollar gold piece. "I can't take it after all, unless one of these gentlemen can change this piece," said I, regretfully. Imagine my amazement when, after one keen glance at my "eagle," the Chinaman dived down his sleeves and brought out a double handful of silver, counted nine dollars and fifty cents out of the pile, took my gold piece, handed me the cane, and turned away with a placid smile and a bow, amid the shouts and laughter of my companions. The lieutenant then offered me his arm and took me to a neighbouring shop, where there was a shelf full of sword-canes just like mine, for twenty-five cents apiece! A BOOT COMPANION.—Mr John Rolfe. Champion Bicyclist of Au, Alia, writes to the Argus. ?Seib iurne, that in the six- days coal est for the championship, after riding 8 consecutive Loire each day, his limbs became stiff and sore, and lie is post- bye be won the great race, and was enabled to ride another 100 miles against time immediately afterward, from the effects prolured by the use of St. Jacobs Oil, in training and racing. He call., it his boon companion and recommends it to all atti- le'es. It c mquers pain and cures rheumatism Price, Is 81. Chemists and Dealers.--Advt. •

div.head: EXAMINER, SA TURDAY,,APRIL 25, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURDAY,,APRIL 25, 1885.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI-
CULTURE, Sec.

Rolland farmers, who have good pasturage and take proper care of their stock, obtain from well-bred Friesian cows an average of twenty-one quarts of milk per diem, and from fresh milch cows twenty-six quarts, although in some extraordinary cases as high as forty-two ipae,rts

per diem has been olkained. MILKING PERIOD.—The period rpf milking may be classed in three parts. For the first six to seven weeks after calving the 'largest quantity of milk per day is produced. After This the yield falls off pretty consider- ably, hut then remains at abovit the same figure for two or three month., when a steady decline sots in until the cow is perfectly dry. By care the best parts of the , milking perioes may be prolonged, and this ought to be the aim of all milk producers. If green fodder and other food, which stimulates milk secretion, can be used at the right time, a ceniderable extra quantity of milk may be produced. RHEUMATISM IN Farm Rorisgs.—Much depends upon what the malady was caused by, or rather what upset the system. It not unfrequently follows influenza and other debilitating diseases, and in such a case the object must be to build up the impaired health of the animal. Tonic medicine and nutritious food must be supplied, and an occasional diuretic may also be given. Carrots would supply the latter, and would prove as wholesome and nutritious food as could be given. Oats, a few beans, and some sweet hay or clover will be proper diet until green food comes in. In the acute stage warm fomenta- tions must be applied locally and shortly followed with such stimulating liniments as vinegar of cantharides. Sometimes this troublesome ailment attacks animals in apparent health, and then much more active means must be taken. It will be needful to call in a veterinary surgeon immediately. The liver and kidneys must be stimulated into working order. Half a drachm of calo- mel and opium, combined with three drachms of aloes, should be at once administered, followed in a day or two by diuretics. The parts must be fomented with warm fomentations, and blistering must follow. In these latter cases the patient must be kept quite quiet. The only food allowed must be bran mash, carrots, and such soft food. Draughty stables or a chill after excessive perspiration is liable to oausethe disorder. THE HISTORY OF A COMPENSATION SCALE—AS a rule • scales of allowance to be used under the Agricultural Holdings Act, adopted in several counties, have not been ;given in this journal, because they are all infringements of the principle of the Act—payment tor results. But the history of the framing of one of these scales is interesting, enough to be given briefly. A discussion has been going on for many months in Nottinghamshire in reference to a scale. At the request of the Notts Cham- ber of Agriculture the valuers met, drew up a scale, and presented it to the Chamber as being the scale generally in force in the county and in accordance with the best agreements. The landowners and their agents declined to adopt it, and proposed a committee to consider it, the committee to be composed of three landowners, three valuers, three agents, and three tenant farmers. The valuers objected to theecomposition of the committee on the ground that valuers should be neutral, but without effect. However, the committee met twice and made four alterations, the valuers objecting to any more. They then met again, the valuers, with one exception, declining to attend, and sixteen other alterations were made, twenty in all, of which nineteen were reductions in compensation to be paid to outgoing tenants, and one increase, for chalking land, never done in the county, as there is no chalk there. This last report was presented to a general meeting of the Chamber on Saturday week, and its adoption was moved by one land agent and seconded by another. The Chairman of the Valuers' Association moved amendments to it clause by clause, and, being supported by a strong party of the most in- telligent farmers, the scale was restored nearly to its original form, as it left the valuers' hands. Then it came out that the reductions had been made for two special purposee--(1) That, being lower than the sur- rounding counties, farmers from those counties will be attractea by having lighter tenant-right to pay; and (2) that this reduced scale would be evidence in a court of law. These points came out in the discussion, which lasted two hours. Notts farmers do not complain of heavy tenant-right if they get what they pay for—con- dition; it is the landlords who complain, because they think that if tenant-right is high, rent must be lowered. —Mark-Lane Express. UCLOVER SICKNHOS AND PCrTASEL—A correspondent writes to a contemporary :—" In 1883, four acres of a 14-acre field, in the occupation of Mr. A. Oldfield, of Grimston, were divided into eight parallel plots, running north and south, each plot oontaining 15 drills of man- gels. The same four acres were again divided into six plots by lines running at right angles over the first named plots, and hence running from east to west. One of these transverse plots (nearly three-quarters of an acre in extent) received at the rate of 2 cwt. muriate of potash per acre, and another of 5 cwt. per acre of kainit. The mangel crop on each plot was carefully weighed and the results meted. Last year, the barley crop which followed the mangels was periodically inspected, and no difference was noticed on any of the plots. This was unexpected by the owner, as two plots had received very heavy dressings of nitrogen for maugels. The bar- ley was uniformly good over the whole 14 acres. Red clover wa.s sown with the barley. The seeds planted well, but during the winter the clover has 'gone off.' Yesterday I again visited this field, being informed by Mr. Oldfield that he should have to plough the field for another crop, the clover having 'gone off' save on three spots. I found a full and healthy plant of clover on a plot in the experimental portion of the field, and another on a distant part, and a very fair plant on another por- tion of the experimental plots. The clover on the rest of the plotted ground, as well as on the remaining por- tion of the field, is so scanty that an ordinary observer would not suppose that clover had been sown. Careful measurement showed one of the very luxuriant plots to be the one where muriate of potash had been sown in 1883; and the other we found to have been the site of a lambing yard five years since. The remaining good plot was that which in 1883 received a dressing of kainit. So strikingly different are these plots from the rest of the field that from a distance they are quite conspicuous, and the boundary of the plots is as marked as it is pos- sible to be. Here is an unexpected but plain proof that, on some lands, the cause of clover sickness is closely connected with the presence or absence of available potash in the soil. Some hundreds of experiments car- ried OR in West Norfolk during the last few years have demonstrated that the soils deficient in potash are more numerous than has been supposed." Packets ONE PENNY and Upwards.—Advt " PRIMROSS DAY."—LORD R CHURCHILL ON THE Go- VERNMENT.—" Primrose Day" was celebrated on Saturday and Sunday by the political followers of the late Earl of Beaconsfield and by their non-political friends who desired to. share in the sentimental observance. There were several social gatherings of Conservatives on Saturday evening, of which the most important was a barquet of the" Primrose League " in St. James's Hall, London. Lord J Manners presided. Lord Randolph Churchill, in proposing the chief toast, said he looked upon the League as the embodi- ment in political energy of the emotions aroused by Lord Beacensiiadla death and the sentiments excited by a know- ledge of his career. Such an association was destined to render invaluable service to the party. For five years they had waited in vain for the promised blessings of beneficial legislation, revived trade, reduced taxation and universal peace. Thousands of lives and millions of British gold had been wasted by the Liberal Government. We were now confronted by a stealthy and ambitious enemy on the north- west frontier of India, and, though he did not desire to in. flame public feeling, he was convinced that until the insidi- ous movement of Russian armies eastward was permanently arrested it would be futile and foolish to hope for any real political and social progress in India under British rule. If England confessed her inability to restrain Russian aggres- sion, our rule in India would have received a mortal blow, and the annihilation of our power would have become but a question of time.—By command of her Majesty, a wreath of primroses was sent to Hughenden on Sunday morning, and , placed on the tomb of the late Lord Beaconsfield by Mrs I Blagden, on behalf of the Queen. THE PREVENTION OF DISEASE. The second item for consideration in the prevention o' disease is that of feeding, with which we shall include water. The importance of the food can be questioned by no one. As we have before said, it is the fuel which keeps,the machine at work. Therefore, it must be constantly sup- plied, or the whole thing will stop. It is not, however, with the necessity for supplying food that we have now to deal. So much is universally admitted. The trouble is that instead of food not being given, it is usually sup- I plied in too great quantities or of too rich and stiinu- ' lating a nature. Infinitely more harm is done from giving too much food than too little, and for one case of the latter we find a score of the former. We may, there- fore, assume that everyone recognises the necessity to give food, and it is our object now to show how the evils resulting from the supplying of too much food, or food unsuitable in quality, can best be avoided.: To take the kind of food, first of all. What the fowl requires is, first, a food that shall supply the daily ex- penditure of force which takes place in every living thing. This expenditure of force varies in fowls as it does in human beings. As the man whose life's work is hard and physically laborious requires food greater in heat-forming qualities than does he whose labour is light; and as the man who lives in a cold climate needs food that will supply the rapid exhaustionrof heat in his body, which exhaustion the resident in warmer spheres does not experience, so it is with fowls. And the food which may be given in one place will be dangerous in another. Not only so, but birds at liberty by the very amount of exercise they obtain, can assimilate and eliminate much richer food than fowls in confinement. But granted all this there can be no question tho plainer the food the better, unless some special object is in view, auch as fat- tening for the tab/e. There is an abundance of choice amongst the grains at our disposal, so that there need not be a level uniformity in feeding. Bread is the staff of life, but we like to have a change, though we return to the bread with all tho greater zest for the change. And we advocate that variety be obtained iii poultry feeding. This is not so important with fowls at liberty as with those whose freedom is restricted. The former find a great variety for themselves, and the grain sup- plied is only a minor part of their diet. In feeding the best method is to stick to the ordinary grains, such as wheat, barley, and oats, reserving such others as maize, buckwheat, and pease for special cir- cumstances. The three former, either in the form of meal or whole grain' mixed or separate, can be regarded as the staple food. And it is not necessary to have the ' very best of these. The small or tail wheat, the small barley, and the common oats, so long as they are sound, really form better food for laying fowls than do the plumper samples. They are rich in the elements which are required, for the floury portions of the •wheat or barley or oat are richer in the qualities which go to make flesh and fat. These are not needed for the forma- tion of eggs, and are, therefore, to be avoided. It is for this reason, namely, the excess of sugar, that •maize or Indian corn is so injurious. The internal organs become coated with fat, and this leads to diseases of many kinds. Also stimulating foods, such as hemp seed, and the un- due use of condiments, cause a straining of the organs, which in time can only result in a breakdown thereof. It is quite possible to give the right kind of food, and yet by giving too much of it, arrive at the tame unde- sirable end as if rich food were supplied. Some there are who argue that the best way is to keep a constant supply of food before the fowls. We were recently upon a farm in the north of France where this was done, the owner declared, with good results. But as the majority of his birds were sold off ore they were a year old, wo do not regard that as sufficient proof of the system. We do not know but that it would succeed on farms where the fowls have unlimited space, especially with the lighter breeds, but in confined runs with any of the heavier varieties we do not think the plan would answer at all. They would eat far too much, and this would cause indolence. We have often given what we regard as the best method of feeding, namely, the supplying of food twice or thrice a day, either on the ground in fine weather, or in troughs when not, and the removal of or ceasing to give more when the fowls appear satisfied. Eating to repletion is always bad, and as doctors tell us we should rise from the table with an appetite, i.e., not actually hungry, but feeling we could out more if we wished to, we should endeavour to apply the seine rule to our fowls, and the doing so will be an effectual pre- vention of over-feeding with its subsequent evils. The giving of tit-bits every now and again during the day is to be deprecated, as is the striving to tempt the appe- tite by dainty dishes. As a rule, we have found that when the appetite of a fowl fails the best method to re- medy this is the withholding of food. It may be offered, and, if not accepted, taken away again. In a day or two nature will right herself, and then plain food will , be the most welcome. The water question is equally important A running stream selves the difficulty at once, but only very few are so favoured as this. If fountains are used they must be kept perfectly clean, and to secure this no fountain should be employed into which the hand cannot be put. Disease is often caused by impure water—disease of the most subtle and deadly character. Water should be often renewed in fountains, and if in open troughs these should not be exposed to the sun. Very often the water supply for fowls is regarded as unimportant, but it has much to do with the health of inmates in a poultry- yard. SEASONABLE HINTS. The weather during the early part of Aprfl has not, we fear, been conducive to successful hatching, and the warning we gave a few weeks ago, and the hints how to act if such a spell of weather as we have had came, will have been very timely. We have heard many com- plaints of trouble with hens, of bad hatching, and of deaths amongst the chicks, but not more than was to be expected with the prevalence of east winds in April. This sort of thing is both disheartening and annoying, but it must be faced with all other troubles. Crying over spilt milk never pays. It may be natural, but the best way is to get more milk. Therefore, if such trouble as we have indicated should have arisen, the best thing to do will be to get some more hens, and try to over- come it in that way. It is not too late to do this yet.

OVERCROWDING IN DUBLIN —Dr. •Cameron has issued a report en the state of the tenement houses in Dublin. It has been ascertained that of the 24,211 inhabited houses in Dublin, 7,234 are occupied by two or more families, and that of the 54,725 families in Dublin no fewer than 32,202 live in the 7,231 houses, which contain 45,116 rooms, thus giving a room and a half on an average to each family, some of whom are twelve in number. The reuts received for the rooms are almost incredible. In four Dublin streets there are 1,071 families occupying 1,482 rooms in 175 houses, for which they pay a yearly rent of £8,311 us, while the houses are valued at £8.677 103. For one house valued at £B, the eight families who occupy it pay £B2 a year rent. Dr. Cameron speaks of Dublin as a decayed city, the worlring-clwses living chiefly in decayed old houses, erected formerly for the nobility and landed gentry classes. In no city in the empire have so many unhealthy houses been closed under the Public Health Act.

WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING. The annual general meeting of the members of the above club was held at the Patten Arms Hotel en Satur- day afternoon and was largely attended. The *hair was occupied by Mr Ashton. The SECRETARY (Ur J R Calvert) read his report, which stated that it was with very great pleasure he brought before them his first annual report. The pleasure was still greater when he had the honour of bringing before them a report which had never been equalled before in the annals of that club. The success they had met with in the season just closed had beeu of the most brilliant description, and had exceeded their most sanguiae expectatioas. It fact, their success was an epoch in the history of that club, and he was confident that they had a grand future before them. Let them go In for unity, for unity was strength, and they could net fail in havieg a still more successful future. (Hear, hear.) Their first team had played during the last season 25 matches, 17 of which they won, 3 had been lost, and 5 drawn. They had scored 12 goals, 28 tries, and 112 minor points against 4 goals, 5 tries, and 37 minor points, scored by their opponents. From this result he could say, without fear of contra- diction, that their club stood next to the Swinton Football Club, which had lost two matches. No club it the county (with the above exception) had lost so few of its aaatohes as the Warrington Club had, and they therefore had every reason to be proud of their first team. They had stuck together like sealing, wax—(langhter)—no going out of town short-handed, or with a poor team—but always with full strength. It had been a pleasure to him to see their first team go out of town. The only fault he could find with them was that when at home they made their oppo- nents wait too long on the field. (Hear, hear.) That, it his °pixies' was ruinous, as spectators did not care to wait an hour before the teams appeared. The following players of the first team had scored in matches :—T Barnes had dropped 6 goals from field of play; J Jolley had dropped x goal; F Tuner and T Barnes had eiteh kicked 2 goals from tries obtaiaed by other players; and W Sprakman had kicked one from a place. J T Massey had scored 6 tries ; J Jolley 5 ; E Gilbert 4; T Barnes 3 ; H Ashton 3 ; I iv Hayes 3 ; F Turner 2; and the following scored Gee each: Warren, Speakman, Frank Turner, Bel- (thaw, Robinson, Davies, Rigby, and Dillon. Every 'man in the team had scored with the exception of the full back, who, of course, they could not expect from his position to score. Taken on the whole, their men had played a grand game all round, and next year he hoped to see them playing a more scientific game, after the experience they had gained when they played against Broughton and Heaton. In the words of the great half back, Payne, they had men of the right stuff; all they wanted was bringing out, and he (the secretary) hoped before long to see Warring. ten olub playing all their crack clubs. If they did not he considered it would be their own fault. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry to say their second team had not had so successful a season as the first. Yet on the whole, all things being eonsidered, they had done fairly welL They had played 19 matched, 9 of which they had won, 6 they had lost, and 4 had been drawn. The scoring had been: 4 goals, 15 tries, and 59 minor points, against 8 goals, 8 tries, and 75 minor points soared by their opponents. It was quite clear their opponents had been better goal kickers, having kicked 8 goals out of 16 tries. Their own men had scored more tries than their opponents, having scored 18, but only kicked 3 goals. But, as he said before, all things being considered, he thought the result credit- able to them, as on many occasions they had gone out of town short-handed, and when with full teams, it was at times only an indifferent one. Next season, however, he hoped to see the arrangemeats for their second team different. It was the intention, as far as practicable, to have (as it were) a stationary team, as the changing of men was directly opposed to the success of the second team. The report then referred to the good attendance of the committee, the proposed change of the club colours,. and the question of the subseriptions.—The Tanastraxa (Mr Pemberton) next read the financial statement, from which it appeared that the total receipts amounted to £l9O los 7d. After meeting the expenditure they had a balance in the bank of £92 135 7il. (Applause.)—Mr Balmuarz. tneved,and Mr Porraa seconded, the adoption of the report, which was agreed to uaanimously.—Mr Foal) and Mr WARREN referred in complimentary terms to the way in which the agars of the clab had been managed by the officers, and it was agreed that an honorarium of £2 103 should be given to the tree- surer.—The following offi :ere for the ensuing year were then elected, via :—Seeretary, Mr J R Calvert ; treasurer, Mr T Pemberton; captain (Ist team), Mr B Warren; sub.captain, Mr W Povey ; captain (acid team), Mr J Whittle; sub-captain, Mr J Boardman; conamittee, Messrs Savage, Turner, Barnes, Jolley, Barnes, jun , Isherwood, Walsh, Davies, and Dillon. This completed the business of public interest. DINNER AND PREiENFATION. In the evening a dinner was held at the same hotel, at which there were between sixty and seventy persons present. The chair was occupied by Conn- oilier Francomb, and there were also present Coun- cillor Ashton, Mr. T. Morris, and Mr. G. Riley. After an excellent dinner had been partaken of, the Seore- tory read letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. C. Broadbent, Aid. Pickmere. and Mr. W. Pier- point.—The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, in proposing the toast of "The Queen and Royal Family," said that as an old football player he took a lively interest in whatever was done by the Club, and it gave him the very greatest pleasure to be there that night. (Applause.) Speaking to the toast, he said they Eaglishmen' or, as he was almost going to say, " Britisher," had some very happy traits in their characters. However much they differed in polities or in religion they still were true to their country and true to their Queen, and at the mo- ment of war they were as one man, and the moment loyalty was required they stood up as a solid mass to support each other. (Applause.) Their Queen had put an excellent example before every mother, every wife, and every woman in this country; and she was beloved, not because she was a Queen, but because she was such a noble woman. (Hear, hear.) They had been inclined to think that the Prince of Wales was going to run some great risks in going across the channel. It was true that in Ireland there had been some sad scenes, but he firmly believed the Irish people were a noble race. (Applause) They had had grievances, and these grievances had been talked about but put off, and that when done for a long time nursed hatred. He was afraid that througla the neglect of their English politicians lots of grievances that might have been remedied had been utterly neglected in Ireland, but he trusted that country had blighter days before it, and that in the future she would be a happy part of the United Kingdom of Cheat Britain and Ireland. (Applause.) —The toast was then cordially honoured.—The Cuirames next proposed "The Army, Navy, and Volunteers." The English soldier, he said, always stood with his face to his foe, and if he had been required to loose his life for the good of his country, from the greatest nobleman to the poorest soldier they had always found them willing to lose it. In the unhappy war they had had in the Soudan Omit' soldiers had approved themselves true warriors, and men who well deserved the thanks and encouragement of those who re- mained at home. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that that war would soon be brought to an end, and that they should lose very few more of their men. (Ap- plause )—Mr Basarasim, in respcnding, said he was sorry that there was not more of the young men of Warrington who became volunteers, because in that way they would derive a great deal of benefit inde- pendent of being of service to their country. (Hear, hear.)—Mr Buxton having sung "Sweet Evelina," The Cnsiesisas said his next duty was to present to their excellent secretary (Mr Calvert) a purse with some gold in it. (Loud applause.) From the manner in which they received the Secretary's name, he could quite see how they thought of him. He (the chair- man) was sure that anyone who had casually met Mr Calvert must have been impressed with his quiet retir- ing way and with his determination to carry out his duties. (Hear, hear„) He must say that if every club had a secretary who studied its interest as Mr Calvert did theirs they would never look behind. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The secretary of a club if he was a good one was the heart and soul of it. (Hear, hear.) Referring to English out-door sports, the Chairman said that he believed that football and cricket and all the physical exercise that the young men of this country engaged in were the things which really made the characters of Englishmen. (Hear, hear.) Young men could never learn to be noble, daring, and brave by stewing in a hot room all the days of their lives. (Hear, hear.) He believed that some of their English officers had learnt how to face danger and how to die on the battlefield by their [ football and cricket in their native laud. He then ' presented Mr Calvert with the purse of gold, and ex- pressed a hope that he would long remain their secretary. (Loud applause.)—Mr CALVERT thanked them heartily for their present being as it was a re- cognition of his services. He fully appreciated the gift, and as he had done in the past so would he do in the future. He should spare no efforts to make the club a success and place it in that proud position which it ought to occupy—that was the top of the tree. (Loud applause.) Mr Alamitos/ proposed the toast of "The Warring. I

ton Football Club." He said he felt proud to propose the success of such a renowned club as that had be- come. He believed it occupied a place in the very front rank in Lancashire, but he should not be satis- fied till they had three or four members in the county team. (Applause.)—Mr Robinson nest gave a hum- orous recitation, after which Mr FORD proposed in complimentary terms "The health of out Captain," to which Ur Asnrox suitably responded—Mr Dillon having sung" Ehrin on the Rhine," Mr T Mortals proposed the toast of the " The officers and commit- tee of the club. He commented upon the success of the club, and said he had scarcely ever known a club have such a favourable balance sheet.—To this toast Messrs Ashton, Pemberton, and Calvert responded.— Mr Warren rang " The sea is England's glory ;" Mr T Barnes gave a recitation, "The burial of Sir John Moore ;" and Mr Ford sang "Down by the river side stray."—Mr T &Limo, in proposing the "Health of the visitors," said that he hoped the time would come when they would, as at Blackburn and other places, have the presence of their borough member at that annual gathering of theirs. (Ap- plause.)—Mr Dillon then gave a humorous recitation, after which the Chairman and Mr Morris responded to the toast, the latter gentleman singing "Rule Brit- tania." Mr J Whittle was recall -d after singing "Mary of Argyle "and then gave 'Tom Bowling."— A vote of thanks to Mr Riley, who had presided at the pianoforte, was moved by Mr Pemberton and respon- ded to by Mr T Mortars prposed a vote of thanks to the club. He had pleasui e, he said, in moving that vote of thanks to Mr Francomb for his straightforward conduct not only in that room but in the parish with which he was connected. (Loud ap- plause.) He could not help saying that to his mind Mr Francomb was like a good soldier, he fought and did not run away. (Rear, hear, and applause.) He hoped Mr Franconab would stick to that good old man the Rector. (Laughter.) Mr Franoonab had taken the bull Ey the horns, and he (Mr Morris) was only sorry he had not been able to throw him over the hedge. (Laughter, and applause.) He hoped, however, Mr Francomb would succeed in what he was trying to do for the well- bsing of his parish.—(Applause.)—The vote was then cordially carried, and the Chairman having suitably responded, a very enjoyable gathering was brought to a close.

NEWTON COMMISSIONERS V. THE WARRINGTON GUARDIANS. At the Warrington County Court on Monday, this case again came en by adjournment, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes.—Mr. Walton, barrister, Liverpool, instructed by Mr. Woreley, law clerk to the Newton Commissioners, ap- peared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Wharton, barrister, Man- chester, instructed by Messrs W. D. Jeans and Co., for the def+ndante. The case was one in which the Commissioners claimed for expenses which had been paid by them on be- had of the Warrington Guardians in respect of hospital attendance and maintenanee of Henry Harris, George Har- ris, Elizabeth Harris, and Alfred Harris, from certain dates mentioned in the particulars. The amount in dispute was £3O Os 4d. At the original hearing Mr. Walton, on behalf of the plaintiffs, said that the Newton Comnsissionere were the Sanitary Authority for the district of Newton-in- Mekerfield, which was within the Union of the defendants, the Guardians. The Corporation of Warrington had a hos- pital for the reception of patients suffering from infectious diseases, and the expenses for which the claim was made had been incurred by the plaint; ffs for the attendance and maintenance of the persons named, who were sent to that hospital from the Newton district. According to an arrange- ment made between the Warrington Corporation and the Guardians the Newton Commiesioners bad to pay for each patient they sent to the hospital at the rate of His per week. The arrangement further was that in pauper cases the expen- ses incurred by the plaintiffs should be repaid to them by the defendants. On the other band, Mr. Wharton contended that there had been no such contract as claimed by the other side, and that the Guardians then, as now, reserved to themselves the right to deal with pauper eases. He also oontended that the cases is question were not pauper cases, and that had they been they should not have been removed without the attention of the Guardians having been previ- ously called to them. After Mr. Wharton had spoken his Honour adjourned the ease, and on it being again called on on Monday, Mr. Walton replied, at considerable length. His case was, he said, that the Newton Commissioners had, at the request of the Guardians, paid monies in respect et matters which were within the scope of the Guardians' dutiee—monies which the Guardians themselves might properly pay—and, having paid them, the plaintiffs were entitled to recover. It was also contended by the defendants that there was no oontract or reqaest, and that, if there was, it was net under sosl and was not binding. Wi:h regard to contract under see', he submitted that it was not required in a case like the one in question, and quoted legal decisions in behalf of that oonteeei ee. 'Living got rid of the neoeseity of a seal, he said, the ordinary law of contract applied. He also remarked that they ha/ sued the Guardians, because they Vans undoubtedly, he claimed, the Rural Sanitary Authority as well.-11,s Honour, in sum- ming up, said that no doubt Mr. Walton's arguments upon certain expressions that had been made use of by Mr. Sut- ton in his letter of the 7th March, 1851, might have some force, but it was well understood that Guaraians could not delegate their duty to other people, and the letter, therefore. *Quid not be so construed. The law was not very clear re- garding the question of the seal, but he must hold that there was no contract. His Honour then gave judgment for the Geardians, the defendants, on all points, also award- ing them costs.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

The bitter wind and piercing frosts we experienced during the latter part of March and the first week of this month have left their mark on some of the garden crops, which look more dismal now than they have done all the winter. Broccoli, cabbage, autumn-sown onions, and cauliflowers have had their leaves browned, Mora or lees, as if they had been scorched. Such has been the extent of this retarding influence, that nice heads of broccoli were cut nearly throe weeks earlier last year than this, and they may be said to be in the same stage now as they were three weeks ago. The hard winds have, however, been moderated by slight showers at the end of last week, and gleams of sunshine for the past two or three days. Fruit buds are likely to benefit from the effects of these retarding agents, so that whatever Injury may have been inflicted on the vegetable crops will, weanticipate, be amply compensated by heavy gatherings of fruit. The late development of fruit buds places them beyond the influence of late frosts which, in the majority of seasons, destroy more or loss of the fruit crops. In consequence of the dry, warm autumn of last year, all fruit trees are bristling with flower buds of plumpest description. Onions: Autumn-sown, if too thick in the bed, should be transplanted on a rich piece of ground, in rows .eight inches distant, and six inches from plant to plant. We cut a few of the longest , roots as well as shorten the tops, and we endeavour to plant them the same _depth as they were beforelbeing pulled up, or rather lifted, for we raise them by thrust- ing a strong stick under each, as they are liable to break just at the neck if not assisted in this way. C.4.1333AGH will be benefited by having the hoe run through them so as to admit air and sun into the soil as well as disturbing the weeds. Some of the earliest show a tendency to " bolt " or form flower stems instead of hearts. They should be pulled up for present use, which will allow more space for those left Tim Faosrr GAIDEIN.—The Lily of the Valley.—Few hardy flowering plants are so highly appreciated as this, i though it is rarely seen growing n cottage gardens. From now to the end of the month is a good time to plant the crowns, either in a clump or by separating them and planting singly two or three inches apart. The latter mode is considered to yield :the finest spikes after the first year. The best implement to plant with is a trowel, such as is used by gardeners. The crowns should be scarcely visible above the soil, and they must be pressed well down with the hands so as to close the soil well round them. They may afterwards have an inch or two of mulching with thoroughly decayed manure or leaf soil, which may be applied annually about this time. The plant is so gioroughly surface- rooting that an inch of fine soil spread over the surface would greatly assist it in the absence of the other ma- terials. From the large breadths we have seen growing wild in woods we feel sure the plants would succeed in many a shady corner where others would not, if they are only annually top-dressed similar to that which nature provides for those growing in woods. Here the leaves from the forest trees fall in autumn so as to cover the ground, and by the time the Lily starts to grow they are partially decayed, and before the end of the season are taken possession of by the roots. English grown roots are so cheap that a clump containing two or three dozen crowns may be purchased for a few pence.. Violets are not so accommodating as the above, though there are not many cottage gardens in the country where they would not thrive and give good return for the labour expended on them. The plant is propagated by division of the roots and seeds. A few of the March flowers left unpicked will form seed pods, which will ripen in time to produce plants which will flower next year. Stronger plants may be had by dividing the roots and planting the youngest portions six inches by eight distant on a fresh dug piece of ground. As to the aspect, we have found them do well on a southern one, and in some instances equally well in an eastern one. Some that we are acquainted with scarcely made any growth this season in a border with a west aspect, which one would 'conclude to be quite as favourable a position as a similar one facing east. THE WINDOW.—Tuberose Begonies will now be fit for potting. Three parts of the old soil should be shaken from the roots; if they have done well in it, imitate as near as possible in mixing up the new. Friable loam three parts and one of decayed leaf soil, with a sprinkling of silver or clean river sand free from saline matter, should grow them well. The size of the pots should be regulated by the size of the tubers, but it is rarely that they require pots of larger size than they have been growing in. It is best to give them only a small space .to grow in at first, and move them into larger pots if re- quired. All window plants should be carried out of doors and laid on their sides on a flag, clean bricks, or a
cloth, and receive a I I good wash by pouring water them, or the leaves may be sponged particles of dust. over

Schedules 7 and 8 having been agreed to, the Bill passed through committee, and progress was re- ported amid cheers. BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE —Mr. BIGGAR then rose to move an alteration in the standing orders of the House, welch should provide that instead of the Speaker deciding when a subject had been adequately discussed, the onus ot so doing should be thrown upon a Minister of the Crown, who, after 1 makings declaration to that effect, should thereupon make 1 a metion that Coe question be now put. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TCESDAY. Lord Redetdale, in the absence of the Lord Chancellor, took his seat on the woolsack at a qux.ter-past four o'clock. THE VOTE OF CREDIT.—EarI GRANVILLE announced that the vote of credit wof.ld be for £ll,ooo,ooo—namelv, £1,500,000 for the operations in the Sondar, and £3,500,000 for the increase of the naval and military services wherever required. It was the desire of her Majesty's Government 'to remain on the most friendly terms with all foreign countries, and this increase in the strength of our naval and military forces did not in the slightest degree diminish the strong desire of a possibility to settle, in an honourable way, all differences which may ordo arise. The Soudan would be held by Indian troops, the British being kept in reserve as an army corps, to be called upon in case of any military emergency. THE Sornati —Lord CLIINBROOIL asked what was the 'intention of the Government with regard to the Soudan.— The Duke of ARGYLL urged that it was the duty of the Govei nment to crush the rebellion and go to Khartoum Lord NAPIER of MAGDALA spoke to the same effect, and the Marquis of RIPON deprecated any farther operations in the Sudan.—The Earl of CARNARNON said that no mention had been made of the expedition in Bechuanaland.—The Earl of MORLEY said that it was not contemplated to remove all our forces from the Soudan.
Aftfr some further discussion. their lordships adjourned at 7.20.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker entered thellouse at twelve o'clock, but a quotum was not made till half an hour later. MISCELLANROTIB.—Sir STAFFORD NouvitcovE, making inquiry as to the future course of public business, took the opportunity of extolling the ability and tact with which Sir C Dilke had conducted the Seats Bill through Committee, a well-merited tribute which was approved by general cheering —ln reply to a further question from the right hon. barunet, Sir CHARLES DILIR said there was no news yesterday with respect to negotiations with Russia.—The second reading of the Irish Registration Bill stood as the first order, and a prolonged discussion was looked forward to. But the debate did not last half an hour, whilst the Scotch Registration Bill wits read a second time without rerdark. The .Municipal Corporations (Ireland Borough Funds) Bill was also read a second time before gentlemen opposed to it had time to regain their breatli. Mr Charles Lewis,having thus missed an opportunity of opposing the Bill, took the unusual course of dividing on the question whether Monday or Thurrday should be fixed for the Committee, but found only live supporters. The next measure was the Sunday Closing Bill, of which Mr. BICRARDtiON moved the second reading without endangering his chances by making a speech. The Speaker had risen to put the question when Mr. WITARTON hurriedly objected, and some conversation took place, with the result that the debate was adjourued. The House divided without a debate on the motion to read the Highways Bill a second time which was carrkd by 87 votes against 28. Sir W. HART•thICE now attempted to put a stop to this extraordinary rapidity of legislation by moving the adjournment of the House, it being close upon half-past three. The motion was not persisted in, and busi- ness went merrily forward, the Barristers' Admission (Ire- land) Bill being read a second time, and several other measures advanced a stage before, at ten minutes to six o'clock, the House adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. . .
_ The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after 4-0. . . .

„. COLONIAL FEDERATION.—EarI GRANVILLE Laving made a short statement respecting the explosion at the Admiralty, the Earl of DERBY moved the second reading of the Ftderal Council of Australasia Bill, and explained that it did not touch upon the greater question of Imperial Federation or even Intercolonial Federation in any complete form, but simply provided for the creation of a Federal Council charged with certain definite duties. Five of the colonies of Australia woe ready to be federated, but New South Wales and New Zealand. refused to join, and if New South Wales continued to stand out it might be a fatal blow to the proposed organisation.—The Bill was read a second time.
EGYPTIAN LOAN BILL.

Earl GRANVILLE moved the second reading of the Egyp- tian Loan Bill.—The Marquis of SALISBURY said the more he studied the BIN the less satisfied was he with the view which the Government had taken or with the considerations they had obtained for the concessions made. He made a strong appeal to the Government to reve,l the intentions they toad as regarded the policy they intended to pursue in Egypt, and to say whether they intended to stay in the Soudan or leave it.—Earl GRANVILLE was glad the noble Marquis had not given effect to the purpose he had shadowed forth a few weeks ago, because it would not only have embarassed us with foreign Powers, but would have done exactly what had been our object to avoid—it would have been an acknowledgment that the guarantee gave the Powers of Europe a right to a control which they did not now possess. On the question of the Soudan, he appealed to the noble Marquis whether en calm reflection he thought it would be wise and expedient in the publia interest for them to exactly specify and define the course they proposed to take. Some reticence ought to be shown, and the Oppo- sition oug t not to press them to do that which might be extremely inconvenient to the nation.—The Iii;1 was read a second time. Their Lordships adjourned at five minutes to Seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Turasnay. The Speaker took the chair at 4 0. THE AFGHAN CRISIS.

_ Mr GLLDSTONE stated that it was not intended to lay any further papers connected with the proceedings on the Afghan frontier on the table of the House befo-e asking for the Vote of Credit. In ieply to the question as to what is the exact point at issue between her Majesty's Government and the Government of Almelo, the right lion gentlemen said Mini- sters were engaged in a correspondence of extreme gravity, that to make a complete statement of ita particulars would be I impossible, and that no partial statement could be given with- out the great risk of creating misapprehension, consequently he could not give any further partioulars to the House. In reply to a further question put by the leader of the Opposi- tion. the Prime Minister said that information might reach them between now and Monday of a character which could be communicated to the House, but he could not enter into any covenant on the subject. Referring to the Vote of Credit, Mr Gladstone remarked that care had been taken to state precisely the character of the vote, end what had to be said in justification of it would be forthcoming on Monday. but he was not aware that it would be his duty to state anything that would ri quire prolonged consideration. In a Case of this kind, where the general grounds of the vote were apparent to the world, and where the extreme importance and the manner in whick they were associated with national interests and dignity was universally recognised, his impression was that it would be the disposition of the House to proceed at once to the discussion of it. Upon being asked whether the despatch of M. de Giers, pub- lished in the morning papers, had been rec-ived by her Majesty's Government, Mr. GLADSTONE replied that he Lad not seen it. An inquiry was made by Mr. O'ICELLi whether the Government would postpone the Vote of Credit until they could place before the House full information regard- ing the Penjdela affair, and Mr. GLAnsrostE said such a course would be extremely prejuAicial to the pub- lic interest, and very adverse to the general feeling of the House.

THE EXPLOSION AT TRH ADMIRALTY.—The HONE SECRETARY informed the House that an explosion took place in th'e morning in one of the lower official rooms of the Admiralty. It was clear that the explosive, whatever it was, was placed inside the room. The quantity was small, and the structural damage was al s 1 small. The Aseistant Under Secretary, Mt Swainson, was set I )usly in- jured, but a favourable account had been receicel of his progress. He believed the rumour as to a sonata explosion to be incorrect Om SERVICE Esnatairgs.—The House then went into Committee on the Civil Service Estimates.

Five hours were occupied on the vole for the disturnpik- ing of roads in Scotland—Shortly after midnight progress was reported in order to take the Scotch Registration Bill, on which the House went into committee pro forma.—A similar stage of the Itish Bill was passe', Mr Gibson, who leads the Opposition, not objecting to the Irish members " amusing themselves " if no subs'antisl progress were made. The remaining orders were run through, and at ten minutes to one the House adjnurnEd.

div.head: AFGHAN CRISIS.
div.p: THE AFGHAN CRISIS.
WAR EXPECTED.

ST. PETF.RSTICRO, MONDAY—The hopeful anticipations of the last few days, drawn from the renewal of the nego- tiations between the two Government', have reCeited a rude shock within the p tst twenty•four hours. It is now said that England, though willing to show considerable moderation with regard to the Afghan frontier, does not accept such ex- planation as has hitherto been afforded of the Itenjleh in- cident. Orders were received at Cronstadt on Sunday directing every warship in the harbour to prepare for war, and in obedience to the command 32 vessels hoislel their

flags. CRONSTADT, SIINDAY.—The arming ef the Russian war vessels continues. Orders were issued to-day for all of them to put to sea. VIENNA, MONDAY.---It is reported from Kieff that 30,000 men have been concentrated there, and that the town and the neighbouring heights ars being rapidly fortified. The semi-official Hungarian paper Nentzeh clears the Austrian Government of any intentions of advancing on Salonica. Important news has been received as to the attitude of Russia towards Persia. Prince Doudoukoff Korsakoff has arrived at Baku, and has invited the inhabitants of the Russian province of Lankoran, on the western side of the Caspian, to report their grievances against the Persian frontier authorities, who are declared to be robbers and ac- complices of robber chiefs. These grievances, such as they are, have existed ever since 1828, but it is ouly now that complaints are made. PARIS, SATURDAY.—At a Cabinet Council held to-day, M. de Freycinet communicated to his colleagues some des- patches concerning the question pending between England and Ruseia, which indicated the prevalence of pacific ideas. The Powers are stated to be actively using their influence for the maintenance of peace. A high official in the India Office is said to have ex- pressed the following opinions :—The statements about the surrender of Penjdeh to Russia are altogether unauthorised, and it would be impossible for the English Government to give up Penjdeh in the light-hearted manner the reports of it surrender would suggest. There is no particular value in Penjdeh, and it is quite possible that had the Dtlimita- lion Cammission been allowed to proceed with its work, the place would have been apportioned to Russia. But after the offensive way in which Rt 19814 has seized it, the greatest difficulty has been placed in the way of accession to that Power. Russia, in fact, has been her own worst enemy in the matter through her impatience and greed. As to the sophistry by which it has been attempted to justify the occupation of Penjdeh, the sufficient answer to it is this that at least it never belonged Russia, and that if the mod; of the Delimitation Commission is not proosstisd with, both Russia and Afghanistan have to go back to the boundary of 1812-3, from Viola 3alah toßgrakhs, or else accept the de- cision of the sword. Russia has no more right to advance south of that !bottom Afghanistan to advance north of it.

div.head: CABINET COUNCIL.
div.p: CABINET COUNCIL.

A Cabinet Council, attended by all the Ministers except Earl Spencer, was held at two o'clock on Dimday afternoon at the Prime Minister's, Dewning-streer, and lasted two and a half hours, concluding juet in time to enable Ministers to reach the Houses of Parliament for questions. The des?atch which arrived on F. flay from Sir Peter Lamsden, and sub- sequent melanges received through Sir E Thornton from St. Petersborgh, were considered; but as the former, wliilet further describing the engagement at Penideb, de s not profess to enter upon any comp irison with the Russian ver- sion of the affair, it was still impossible for Ministers to arrive at a foal opinion. This has therefore been deferred. In the supplementary description the British Commissioner repeats and somewhat amplifies the account which he had communicated to the Government in his previous despatch. It is understood that the Cabinet had under consideration the number of the army and militia Reserves to be called our, the amount of the vote of Credit, and also the main proposals of the Budget.
SIR P. LUMSDEN S DESPATCH. DENIAL OF GENERAL KOMAROFF'S STATEMENTS.

The following telegraphed despatch was laid on the table of the House of Commons on Tuesday evening:— Sir P. Lumsden to Earl Granville (received April 21, 8-30 a.m.) .TIRPIIL, APRIL 17, 1885. Your Lordship's telegram of 13th. General Kemaroff's account of attack on Penjdeh is con- sidered incorrect. 1. General Komaroff says. "On the 24th March one de- tachment approached Teel] Kepri, on our bank Of the Kushk." Reply: Tash Kepri is Turki for Pul4-Khisti. General Komaroff's clai.n to eithert bank of Kuelik Is unten- able. The left bank of Kushk has always been held by Afghans, and was never in Russian occupation. On 20th February the Russians located an outpost of 25 Yulatan Tnrcomans at K zit Tepe, a mound one mile north of Pul-i- Khisti, and about same distance from nearest point of Kushk river and from its junction with Morglial). This had al- ways remained the extreme limit of the Russian advance within their line of vedettes. The Russian cavalry detach- ment alluded to did advance against Pul-1-I(histi on the 25th, but retired before reaching that place when warned by the Afghan commander, as on 20th February. 2. General Komaroff states: "Near the bridge I found an intrenchment occupied by Afghans." Reply : This position was occupied by Afghans previous to General KomarofFs advance and to the agreement mentioned in your Lordship's telegram of 17th March. 3. General Komar( ff says: "In order to avoid a conflict I placed my troops five vests from Afghan position." Re- ply : This can only refer to main body, as Ruslian troops were in K'zil Tepe, which is one mile from Afghan position, and the Russian vedettes were considerably in advance of that.

4. General Komaroff says:—" When Afghans bad con. vinced themselves that we had no intention of attacking them they began each day to come nearer to our camp." Reply : So far from Afghans being convinced of General Komaroff's innocent intentions the continued and irritating daily attempts to excite hostility convinced Afghans of Russian determination to provoke conflict, and induced what appeared to them the military necessity of extending their defensive poition. 5. General Korn iroff states:—" On 27th March Afghans sent against one company, which was charged with cover- ing a reconnaissance, three companies with a cannon, and some cavalry." Reply : A reconnaissance in force itself meant hostile intention. A Russian company meant 250 men, more than equivalent to three Afghan companies, ag- gegating 225 men. On 27th two bodies of Russian troops I simultaneously advanced. Colonel Alikhanoff with cavalry pushed past Pul-i-Khisti, and Russian infantry penetrated the right flank of Afghan position on right bank of Mur- ghab. Colonel Alikhanotr only retired when intercepted by Afghan cavalry some four miles in rear of Afghan position, and Russian infantry only when Afghan commander drew up three corapanis and warned Russian officer that if he advanced further he would be fired upon. General Komaroff's chief of staff at the interview of 20th called Colonel Alikhanoff's advance merely a pleasure trip, but was informed that the Afghan commander viewed it in the most serious light. G. General Komaroff states :—" Afghan audacity and arrogance increased by degrees." Reply : It may have been so, but, if so, it was entirely caused by Russian action, as the Afghans did all they could to avoid collision, and it was solely owing to their patience and forbearance during two months of incessant irritation that peace has been pre- served so long. The Afghan commander's courteous reply
of 29ch to General Komaroff's ultimatum proves his wish to the last to avoid conflict.

- 7. aeneral Komaroff says : "Da 28th Afghans occu- pied a height which commanded left flank of our camp, began to throw up intrenchments there to establish a post of cavalry behind our line, and placed a picket at gun shot distance from oar ford." Reply : It was the case that the Afghan commander did on 28th after the occurrence of the hostile reconnsisance on 27th, place a post of observation on the hills on right bank of Margbab, to' give notice of any like fresh Russian advance on that dank, but this post was withdrawn the next day.

8 General Komaroff says : "On 29th I sent to Afghan commander an energetic summons, Sze, and I received an answer that by the advice of the English he refused to re- tire across the Kushk." Reply : The fact itself is reported to me to be totally incorrect, and nowhere in the Afghan commander's reply is any such statement. On the contrary, the wording is distinct—" I have daly received your letter regarding the withdrawal of certain pickets. As I had re- caived orders from the Governor of Herat to consult Captain Tate, who has been deputed to Penjdeh by Sir Peter Lums- den in such matters, I showed him your letter. Captain Tate afterwards had as interview with Colonel Zakrcbew- ski and informed me of the conversation which had taken place between them. Be it known to you that I must loy- ally obey the orders I have received from His Highness the Ameer. I can in no way go anything contrary to the orders of my Sovereign. Of course in matters of detail, such as alterations in positionrof advanced pickets and vedettes pas- ted in front of the troops, I am prepared to come to an arrangement with you with a view to the avoidance of any risk of conflict."

9, General Komaroff says : "I again addressed a private letter couched in friendly terms." Reply : The letter in question was never seen by any officers of the Commission, but Captain Delashoe was told that a letter had been re- ceived a few hours before Russian attack on 30th. I have now called on Sepeh Sslar for copy of second letter." _ _

10. General Kemaroff states : " On 30th, to support my demands, I marched with my detachment against the Afghan position, counting still on pacific result, but artillery fire and cavalry attack compelled me to accept combat." Reply : Russians advanced to attack of Afghan position and of course Afghans were obliged to defend themselves. Cer- tainly the engagement was not commenced by artillery fire as stated by General Komaroff, as infantry firing was heard continuing several minutes before the first gun.
