div.head: M. DE GIERS' DESPATCH.
div.p: M. DE GIERS' DESPATCH.
A Balla netraspondest sapplies what is represente3 te be the text el X. de Gists' despatch to the Russian Ambassador in London, as follows : St. Petersbury, Marah_3l, 1895.

(AngliCe. April 12.) The telegram from G eneral Komaroff, of which I have jest transmitted to you the tenor, furnishes the desired cx. planations with regard to the facts which led up to the last incident. We have nothing to add to it, but we make an appeal to the wisdom of the British Calo'net to appreciate the situation, of which this incident has revealed the char- acters and the dangers. It is Impossible for us not to trace back the c wee to the military aspect with which the Eng- lish Government thought it their duty to invest their Boundary Commission. From the iusttnt when we fist received an account of the escort which accompanied this Commission I pointed out to Sir Edward Thornton the grave difficulties to which it was likely t 3 give rise, and . I renewed this observation in measure as the originally moderate strength of the escort increased. Our friendly remonstrances were not listened to. It, was, however, easy to foresee that the Afghans would see in the apparition of this military .niseion a pro- mise of support and encouragement in their pretensions and their covetousness. We do not wish to inquire too closely into the nature of the activity at the Eng:ish Commission, but we cannot pass by the facts that certain officers in its suite directed the movements of the Afghan troops, and that the loudly proclaimed interview between the Ameer and the Viceroy and its bellicose surroundings must certainly have contributed, to embolden the Afghans to the point of com- mitting such acts of provocation as could not be tolerated by the representatives of Russian military authority without failing in the discharge of their duty. The sole co-clusion that we wish to draw is the urgent necessity of putting an end to an equivocd situation which is not without danger. We continue to think that the last incident ought nor to stop the negotiations which have for their aim the consoli- dation of good relations between the two empires. (Signed) DE USERS.

div.head: WAR PREPARATIONS.
div.p: WAR PREPARATIONS.

Mr Dunn, the Chief Constructor of the Navy, paid his first visit to the Cunard liner Umbria at L'verpool on Mon- day. This steamer only reached the Mersey on Sunday, and the inspection was of a very preliminary kind. The Etruria, sister ship to the Umbria, is now flee t) depart. aud leaves the Mersey on Saturday next on her maiden voyage. The work on bead the Oregon is being completed with great rapidity, The America Is merely waiting for the arri- val of the guns to enter on her new occupation. A confidential message just received by the Portsmouth nivel authorities points to the immediate commissioning of a powerful fleet and other extraordinary preparations of a warlike character. All the thirteen gunboats are to be com- missioned, a torpedo flotilla is to be got ready for urgent eervice, as well as the artnourclads reported fit for duty, without delay. The orders received are of a most urgent character, and will necessitate the ceiling up of the Naval Reserve and the Coastguardernen. Large supplementary grants will be made. Orders were recoived at Portsmouth on Saturday to commission at once the three gunboats Weasel, Pike, and Snap, all of the Comet class. Ordere were also received to complete the defect." of the Inflexible within six weeks. Any repairs that will tike longer are ' not to be begun. Orders were received at Portsmouth on Monday to launch the whole of the seventeen gunboats lying on the slips at Heger, and coal, provision, and com- mission them. The first consignment of 300 torpedoes ordered from a firm in Germany will arrive in this country daring the pre- sent week. A portion will be distributed to ships for their use, and the remainder conveyed to British ports which would be in danger of attack in case of hostilities. The Vienna Politische is informed from Odessa that con- siderable war preparations are being made by Russia at Batoum, and two warships are plying between the two ports carrying heavy position guns' ammunition, and other war materials. The balbou is being armed, and considerable forces ate concentrating with the object of securing the Poti-Tiflis railway. There is similar activity at Kertch and Yenikale. The fortifications erected after the late war at the foot of the MithridA mountain have been armed with guns of the strongest calibre, and several strand batteries have been mounted in the Gulf of Kertoh. The St. Peters- burg correspondent of the official Weiner Zeitung writes that within a few weeks the Russian army in Central Asia will unmber 1('0,000 men, besides 25,000 Turkomans organised like Cossack', aqd an equal number of Tarkoman sharpshooters. The Vienna papers are more alarmed by the sudden outbreak of violent article in M. Katkoff's paper, the Moscow Gazette, and the Russian military organs than by the news from London. . - -

A supplementary estimate issued on Thursday mentloas 35,000 as the number of men of all ranks required for army service, besides the number already voted. An Exchange Company's telegram, da'ed Paris, Thurs- day, 10 am , states :—lt is stated that the Russian war ships in the Mediterranean have been ordered to cruise on the coast of Italy, the object being to overawe the Italians against joining England in the event of a war with Russia.

A Central News telegram, dated Berlin, Thursday, states: —I am informed on reliable authority that King Oscar of Sweden, on leaving this capital, declared that in the event of hostilities between England and Russia Sweden would maintain the strictest neutrality.

The occasion for the postponement of the Budget is ex- plained in the Haase of Commons from two points of view. On one side it is stated that the relations with Russia are so strained that it is important to secure the passage of the Vote of Credit without an hour's delay. On the other hand

It Is asserted that as there still remain hopes of a pacific settlement, the Chancellor of the Exchequer is anxious not to bring in a War Budget unnecessarily. There are three ways of providing for the extraordinary war expenses involved in the Vote of Credit. The first is by postponing payment, as was done by the late Govern- ment, in order to meet war expenditure: the second is by suspending the operation of the Sinking Fund ; and the third by taxation. The first is an expedient which the present Government will certainly not adopt, and it is probable that the financial position will be met by a combination of the two latter courses. . . . .

The Press Association is in a position to state that the farther cornmunicitions received from Russia are to the effect that the St. Petersburg Gov..rnment will not make env further inquiries into the statements in General }Coma- rofFe report. The opinion in both English and Russian diplomatic circles is that peace cannot be maintained. The Daily _News says :—We understand that though no definite conclusion his been come to, sitisfactory arrange- ments with Turkey in the event of a war with Russia are probable. Fehmi Pacha is believed to be well pleased with the result of his mission to this country. We .re able to give a positive contradiction to the statement published on Wednesday in some of our evening contemporaries to the effect that General Ignatiaff is in correspondence with Mr. Gladstone with regard to the maintenance of peace. There is absolutely no foundation for this assertion. WAR IMMINENT.

It is stated that at the Cabin.t Council held on Tuesday, Sir Peter Lumsden's detailed statement of the affair at Penj- deb was considered, and that an important desnatch was transmitted to Sir Edward Thornton for communication to the Government of the Czar.

The gravity of the sittittion as estimated by Ministers was indicated in Parliament on Tuesday night by the fact I that both Earl Granville and Mr Gladstone were furnished with manuscript containing an identical statement, which, contrary to Parliamentary usage, they read to the respective Howse. It was noticed that in their references to the °c- andor' of tbe vote at credit neither Lord Granville nor the I Prime Minister made open references to Russia. Mention was made of the desirability of having a the fighting re- sources of the country ready for action "wherever they might be required ;" and, as far as the disposition of money was concerned, it was alluded to as being required for "special preparations." THE BATTLE ON THE KUSHK.

Further details have come to hand of the fighting on the Kustik, and the decided tendency of this later information Is to place the action of the Russians In an infinitely worse light than did our previous knowledge of the incident. The fight it is now certain was of a very desperate character indeed, notwithstanding that the Afghans were so greatly out- numbered. What they lacked in numbers, however, they made up in bravery, fighting splendidly until the last, when the superior strength of the Russians compelled them to ttke flight. The Afghan General worthy example to his troops, and was throughout in the foretroui of the, fight- ing, being twice wounded.

div.head: SOITD XN CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE SOITD XN CAMPAIGN.
FURTHER ADVANCE.-BURNING OF HASHEEN.

Telegrams from Lieut.-Gen. Sir G. Graham— " &AKITA, SATURDAY, 7-45 P —Made reconnaissance in force on Hasheen,Deberet, and Valley of Khor, Aber, leaving camp at five this morning with two regiments of cavalry. Horse Artillery, fifty Mounted Infantry, and 15th Sikhs. Column from Handoub composed of Australians, Mounted Infantry, and screw guns, moving on Deberet, by pass through Maratab Hills. Mounted Infantry and native scouts operating from Otao towards some point supported by half battalion Scots Guards. At seven o'clock passed Dibelbat. Bengal Cavalry scouting in front and 20th Hue. ears on right. Reached Deberat at nine o'clock. Few half- filled wells, water three feet surface. Handonb column oc- cupied mouth of pass, and Otao column low hills in front of Khor Aberet. Parties of enemy seen by Mounted In- (entry retiring southward. Retired force at eleven, burning village of Hasheen, which showed signs of recent occupa- tion ; no cattle seen. Reference to my telegram 15:h prisoners released, cattle kept." " SUAKIX, MONDAY, 8-20 P.M.—TAM/SOUK, NOM—Just arrived. This post held by General Fremantle, with Scots Guards, two screw guns, end company of Engineers. Otao held by battalion Coldstream, with company of Mounted Infantry. The pesition at both places strong. No signs of enemy. Health of troops excellent. Water supply at Otao abundant and fair quality. Does not taste brakish, but will get analysis." THE REVOLT AGAINST THE MAHD I. CAIRO, MONDAY.—The English colonel in command of the Engineers, together with several officers, left this place yesterday evening for Alexandria at very short notice, and on what is understood to be special service. It is believed that they have gone to inspect the fortifications. The rebel troops have left Beth i and Sani for Berber, which is in open rebellion against the Mandi. Tne rebellion, Which is under the leadership of a Sheikh namad Megamtni, had its origin in a quarrel about the treasure. DONGOLA, MONDAY. - The thermometer registers 112 degrees in the shade to-day. According to information obtained fran native sources, the Italian trosps have advanced from Massowah, in the direction of Kassala. The Arabs on the White Nile above Khartoum are said to be deserting the Mandi, who is robbing everyone of any- thing worth seizing.

div.head: RAILWAY OPERATIONS.
div.p: RAILWAY OPERATIONS.

The Pall Man Gazette says the Government have de- cided not to persist in pushing the caropAign against she Mandl as far as Khartoum. Osman Diva now being de- cisively smashed, the railway will be pushed forward to Tambouk or Sinkat. Beyond that point the railway will not be made, at least until the hot weather is over. The balk of General Graham's forces wilt be withdrawn, as well as those on the Nile, as soon as circumstances will permit. SUAKIN. WEDNESDAT.—It is probable that General Gra- ham's head-quarters and the troops now here will remain at Snakim math the railway reaches Otao in about a week hence, when they will move direct to Otao. The Camel Corps is expected to be formed In three days, when a recon- naissance will be made of Essybikl from Tambuk. Many more natives have signified their desire to submit to the British. General Graham is endeavouring te induce the natives to federate among themselves against Osman Digma independently of the British. THE SLAVE TRADE AT KHARTOUM.

--- --- Dowoota, THITIZSDAY.—A messenger who has arrived here from Khartoum reports a brisk sale of captured slaves at that place, and states that the Christians taken prisoners by the Mabdi hare been sent to Abbah Island. lie confirms the news that Kassala and Senaar continue to bold Out. StrAlEUtie TIIIIRSDAT.—A portion of the newly-formed Camel Corps left here at daybreak this morning, and was iexpected to arrive at Handub at eleven am. General Gra:. ham will proceed to Tambuk to-morrow, returning here in the evening.

what gloomy view of the future, but it is not because he thinks the people of India have their eyes constantly upon Russia; it is be• cause Englishmen at home know so little, and therefore trouble themselves so little about the great Empire whose destiny is in their hands. India is not to be strengthened as a British Dependency by absorbing for war purposes funds set aside for insurance against famine, or by gagging the native press as was done by the late Government. It was urged when the present Administration pro- posed to remove restrictions on the press, that they were opening the door to discon- tent and disloyalty, and that another mutiny might be expected. We know too well the bitter hostility which Lord RIPON had to encounter through giving his support to the Ilbert Bill—a measure founded on the sim- plest principles of justice; while he met with all kinds of opposition from Anglo- Indian officials in his efforts to extend the principles of local self-government. He has given the people a foretaste of freedom, and we are not, as was predicted, in the throes of a revolution. Even Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has to admit that the natives are loyal—loyal because, for a brief space at any rate, they have been treated with something like fairness. Let us keep them loyal by dealing justly with them; by putting them on an equality with out selves before the lax; by leaving them, where it can be done, to Manage their local affairs by local men ; by giving them, generally speaking, more repre- sentation with less taxation. Let us be just and fear not; and India, instead of being a thorn in our side, will become a tow-r of strength and a present help in the hour of need.

CHURCH matters in Earlestown continue "lively," and the " scandal " still exists if the row about it is not so great as it was some time ago. The Rey. G. Lovarr, who is acting as curate for the Rev. T. R. MATTHEWS, the vicar of the church of St. John the Baptist, is comparatively new to the parish, and he does not like the state of affairs being described as a scandal. He says :—" Whatever scandal there was last year, there was none whatever at the last vestry meeting." Opinions doubtless differ as to what is a scandal, and clergymen in such matters are notoriously case-hardened. For our part, we cannot but think it was a scandal upon the Church that, through some- body's negligence, insufficient notice had not been given of the very meeting Mr. LOVETT refers to, and that, consequently, the whole proceed- ings have been found to be illegal. Further, it was a scandal upon the Church that no minute-book was forthcoming when business should have commenced; and that the par- ishioners were not permitted, according to custom, to elect the organist, for whose services they are called upon to pay. But the most scandalous thing of all, as it seems to us, was revealed in the fact that there was no message of peace from Mr. MATTHEWS as a ' preacher of peace. And that is how the case stands to-day. The second vestry meeting— it is to be hoped it will be a legal one this time —was held on Monday last; and the missing minute book "turned up." But for all prac- tical purposes it might just as well have re- ; mained amongst the lost sheep ; for when it was opened it was seen that there was no re- cord in it of the vestry meeting of the pre- vious year ; so that as no minutes were entered there were none to confirm. When it came to a question of passing the accounts, nobody 'could say what the balance was at ; the commencement of the year, the Chair- man getting over the difficulty, after a fashion, by saying he would not take upon ' himself to say anything about it. Is this not a scandal upon the Church, or are we to understand that it is "a pious opinion" of the Church that irregularity as to balances is commendable ? When the question was I raised as to appointing the people's warden, BIRKHEAD was proposed for the office, but that gentlemen promptly declined the dubious honour—" if he had only to be a collector of money' He wished to know if the parishioners were to be permitted to ap- point the organist, as had been the custom prior to Mr. MATTHEWS turning his back upon his people. On this point the Curate, , as Chairman and Vicar's Deputy, read a letter from the Bishop's Secretary to the effect that the appointment rested with the I Vicar, and that "the vestry have no power whatever to interfere with the i 1 appointment." It was in vain that Mr.• ; BIRILHEAD and Mr. Cortmerr pointed out that, in requiring that the appointment 1 of organist should be made by the pari- shioners, they were "doing what had been done ever since the church was established." They Were in effect told that if Mr. MAT- THEWS had made a concession, Mr. , MATTHEWS could withdraw the concession. !Et would, therefore, seem that in the past he has been humouring them as so many spoiled children; he has been letting them play at appointing the organist, all the time serenely conscious that he could snap his fingers and stop the game whenever he thought fit. Power of appointment They have no power to do anything, except to pay; and when they have done that they do not seem to be able to get a satisfactory statement as to what becomes of the money. It was brought out that the sum of 2.c00 was invested for keeping the church fabric in repair; and it was stated that two years' interest was 'due. But there was "nothing in the accounts about it and the chairman, when appealed to, said it was a matter on which he could ..give no information. He was frank enough to say that " all public mbney should be accounted for publicly ;" but he does .not seem to see that the absence of an account in these cases—for such sins of omission are not confined to Earlestown—constitates in each instance a scandal upon the church. Fortunately, as Shakespeare has it, there is a soul of good in things evil, and tle good that is coming of these evil things is the cry for reform which is being raised within the Church itself—reform which must end in freedom of the Church and freedom off the People from the corrupt and blighting influence .of State contro'.

THERE was nothing to report to Parlia- ment last night with regard to the all-absorb- ing question of Peace or War with Russia. Lord FITZISAKTRICE declined to say whether the despatch was authentic which is given in our news columns as having been sent by M. de Giers on behalf of Russia. Hit be authen- tic, there is little likelihood, we regret to say, of peace being preserved, the situation at the present moment being' in the words of the Prime Minister, one of "extreme gravity." Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to a question put by Mr. RICHARD, said nothing had taken place in the correspon- dence between England and Russia to the prejudice of arbitration. Beyond ,this, he could not, of course, say anything, see- ing that any indication of weakness just now

div.head: 'ME EXAMINER S,ATURDA Y. APRIL 25, 1885.
div.p: 'ME EXAMINER S,ATURDA Y. APRIL 25, 1885.

would have the effect of hardening Russia in the attitude she has assumed. But there is no reason why the country should not speak out on the question of arbitration, and we trust that, before the worst comes to the worst, the matters in dispute will be referred to an outside and independent authority. If Russia means war, a proposal of this kind will prove abortive ; but in the interests of hu- manity it should be made before resorting to the direful shock of arms.

Charles Ralok- lutski, a Pole, who had been employed at Messrs Hutchin- eons' chemical works, and who lived in Eleanor-street, was brought before Mr. T. S. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, as a dangerous lunatic. When being led into court he shrieked and yelled in a fearful fashion, and made frantic efforts to escape from the six constables who sur- rounded him. Detnoniacil fury was in his eyes, and he glared upon the officials and persons in the court in quite a murderous fashion. Mr. Scannell deposed that on Satur- day evening the man attempted to enter a house in Eleanor- street with a knife in his hand, threatening to murder the inmates. His conduct in the street was also most danger- ous, and he gave him into the custody of the police. In the cell at the station, tha man shouted continually that there was something eating his heart away, and he spent most of the night in oraying.—Dr. Cooper certified that the prisoner was a lunatic dangerous to himself and to those about him and his Worship committed him to Rainhill Asy- lum.

From a statement by Inspector Wood, it , appeared that for the rest roar months the prisoner had lodged at the San Inn. Aboat half-past ten o'clock on Sun- day night, Mrs 'Amax placed £7 lOs in her purse, which she put into the pocket of her dress. The dress was hang- ing behind her bedroom door. Sometime during the night Mrs Lomax heard the jingling of money, bat she took no notice of it. The Chairman thought Mr Deacon had male Out a good case.—Dr O'Keeffe suggested a postponeeneut of the ques- tion. It would be unfair to deal with the matter before the members had had time to carefully consider it.—The Rev Father Finegan saw many objections to the proposal. He thought the less the Board wont out of their way to harems persons engiged in teaching and the better it would be. It certainly appeared to him grotesque ter the School Board to examine private schools. He thought the country owed a great deal to private schoole. It was not long sinca the edacation that was curled on rested upon the shoulders of those persons whom Mr Deacon now wished to sup- press.—Mr Deacon : No, no.—The Chairman : Hardly that, Father Finegan. Father Finegan : I will say inspect, then. The children attending apse schools were composed ef a class socially between those at- tending public' elementary schools and those who were educated in colleges, or were under the instruction ef pri- vate tutors. One of the great reasons why such persons sent their children to private schools was, be thought, be- cause in many instances they were supposed to have a better tone than the ordinary elementary school ; and because they were not overpressed and driven in order to pass a severe examination. He therefore did not think the Board ought to interfere with the parents preference. He was prepared to grant that some of the schools were not up to the mark. but at the same time he would rather leave them alone, than do what would be considered in the eyes of the persons Interested as cruelty.—Mr Glover thoucbt Father Finegan had misunderstood the position in which the Edecation Committee was placed. It was a duty they could not avoid —to see that the -elementary educ Ilion throughout the en- tire neighbourhood was efficient. The committee did not wish to interfere with the private schools. They were in favour of these schools being in the neighbourhood, conduc- ted on right princrples, and the committee only offered them inspeetien. If he were a private school teacher—of course be might be some day—(laughter)—he should wel- come this inspection, and especially the certificate, which he would use as an advertisement. (Hear, hear.) Father Clarks bslieved that the education in most of the private schools was very good, and he thought if the masters kept a register of the attendance of the chilli-en it would meet the object the committee had in view.—Mr

SOUTH•WIST LANCASHIRE. The Liberal Association for the lace Division have adopted Mr. C. Percy, mining and mechanical Engineer, of Wigan, as the labour candi- date of the party. Mr. N. Eckersley will be the Conserva- tive candidate.

WIGAN.—Mr. F. S. Powell, who was returned for Wigan. on Lord Lindsay taking his seat in the Upper House, but who was afterwards unseated, will be adopted as the Con- servative candidate. Mr. G. H. Lea, of London, will be the Liberal candidate.

MANCHESTER AND SALFORD. SOrae progress bas been made in the choice of Parliamentary candidates for Man- chester and Salford. Mr. Holdsworth elects to stand for the North-West or Central Division, Mr. %Boar for the East or Ardwick Division, and Mr. Jacob Bright has provisionally consented to contest the Western Llulme Divieion, and Mr. Slagg's name has been connected with the North-Western Division. In Salford the Liberal candidates are Mr. A. Arnold, M.P ,Mr. B. Armitage, M.P., and Mr. W. Mather. The Con•ervatives have selected as two of the candidates Mr. T. G. Bowles and Mr. E. Hardcaatle.

Mr W Agnew, M.P., will contest the Stretford Division, and Mr R Leake, Ml', the Radcliffe Division in tho Liberal interest. At Birmingham the Conservatives have decided to con- test each of the seven seats, but Ihe cAndidates' names will not be officially made known until the Conservative demon- stration on June 24th, 25h, and 26:h. It is announced that, if selected, Lord R Churchill would be willing to contest Central Birmingham, in opposition to Mr Bright. Sir W Lawson has been conditionally adopted by the Cen- tral Liberal Committee of the Cockermouth Division of Cumbarlandas their candidate.

The Hon Bernard ColerLige will contest in the Liberal interest the Attercliffe Division of Sheffield. Tbe Conserva- tives are in Communication with Mr H Vincent to become the candidate for the Central Division. Lord Edmund Fiumaurice has been invited to stand for North Hackney, as the Liberal canlidate. At a mceting of the Council of the South Manchester (Hulme) Liberal Association, bad (n Wednesday evening., Mr Jacob Bright, Ml'., was chosen at the candidate i'or the division at the next general election.

GLADSTONE ON TILE FRANCHISE Acr.—Replying to a Lincolnshire correspondent, the Premier says that under the Franchise Act of last year every min in England °ace- pylng a house, of whatever value, will be entitled to be registered as a voter, if he fulfil, the conditions set forth in Section 3 of the Representation of the People's Act 1867. 111/3 WAR PROSPECT AND LOCAL TRADE.—We under- stand that Mr Edward Bolton, of the Flint Glass Works, Warrington, has secured a large Grevernment order for goods that are ohiefly intended for use in war steamers, and that the Warrington Wire Rope Works (20, Limited, have received a large order for torpedo wire netting. The news has been I received with some satisfaction, as it will materially tend for the time to improve the trade of the locality. JOSEPH MAZZINI, a memoir by E. A. V., with two essays by Mazzini : (1) "Thoughts on Democracy ;" (2) "The duties of man," No pecuniary profit is desired from this publication ; but it is hoped that this eloquent memorial of a noble patriot and a good man may awakes a true patriotic enthueiasm in the hearts of many young English readers; and that the principles set forth may help to the formation of wise and just political opinions. People's edition with portrait, price 61. To be obtained from JOHN S. dIiREN, Bookseller, &c., 34, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. ALLEGED HORSE STEALING AT WIDNBB.—A man named Wm Hewitt was charged, at the Warrington Police Court, on Friday, with having been drunk in Winwick-street on the previous evening; and also with having stolen a borse,a saddle, and a bridle, belonging to E Award l'ercy, from Widnes, on Tnesday.—lt was stated by P.C. 14 that on the previous evening he was informed by Percy that the prisoner was at Town's-end, and that be had stolen a horse, saddle, and a bridle belonging to him from Widnes. Tim officer apprehended the prisoner, who was drunk, and he admitted having taken the horse and sold it for £5. He bad £2 16s 6d in his possession, which was what remained of the price of the horse.—Prisoner was fined Sc and costs for being drank, and it was directed that he should be handed over to the county police on the other charge. There were cheers for Mr Gladstone and local Libetals throughout. After Mr Tollemache, M.P., had, with extreme difficulty, made himself heard, Mr St. John Corbett rose to speak. For some minutes he was dnable to make himself beard. Wax- ing indignant at the frequent interruptions, Mr Corbett shook his fiat and exclaimed at the top of his voice, " Gentlemen, I say that the nations on the Continent don't care a-- about England." A perfect roar of laughter and hooting followed this outburst. Mr Corbett eventually apologised ; but the subsequent speaker, Dr Mackie (War- rington), refused to face the meeting, which was marked by extraordinary scenee to the elm," Loud. CA'..OlB AT CHYSTI3II Asetees —The business of these As6i6iii WM resumed on Monday morning, Mr Justice Field again presiding.—An Unnatural Offence.—George R (22), labourer, pleaded not guilty to an indictment charg- ing him with an unnataral offence at Rune wn, en the 7th March. He NMI found guilty, and sentenced to ten years' penal servitude.—An Unnatural Father.—William Dean, 37, labourer, pleaded guilty to indecently assaulting bit own daughter Mary, twelve years of age, at Walton Inferior, near Warrington, in December last. His Lordship passed sentence of two years' imprisonment with hard labour. -- Sentences on Tuesday For maliciously wounding Mary Tracey, at Widnes, on the 14th tilt, Peter Riley (23), labourer, was sentenced to three months' im- prisonment; Mary dorley (40), was sent to prison for nine months, and Mary Eyres (39), for three months, for s"eating a watch and chain belonging to James Heath, at.Widnes, on the 4th lust.

CONFIRritATION SERVICE AT RI7NCORN PARISH Caunon. Yesterday the Lord Bishop of Chester held a confirmation service at Runcorn Parish Church. There was a large con- gregation present to watch the ceremony, and the following clergy took part :—The Revs W Preston, J Lockwood, E M Armson, J J Bryant, R Edwards, and J Madden. The Rev Canon Barclay occupied a seat in the chancel. There were 206 persons presented for confirmation, distributed as fol- lows :—Parish Church 79 females, 54 males ; Trinity Church 18 females, 12 males ; Halton Church 18 females, 7 males ; Weston Point Church 11 females, 6 males. There was also one female from Northwich —His Lordthip ad- dressed the confirmees at considerable length. He explained that they were there to renew the promises made for them by their god fathers and god mothers, and that after being confirmed they would have the right to come to the table of the Lord and p 'mike of the holy communion. They must know that from the age of 12 years to 16 years boys and girls went through very great changes, not only with re- gard to their bodies, but with regard to their minds, and they became young men and young women. New powers came to them which they were in danger of being tempted to'rnisuse. They were entering upon a new coantry, and beginning a new battle against the enemies of their soul, who appeared in new forint; and with new weapons, and they required to be newly armed by God their Saviour to withstand and conquer the enemy. He should therefore pray for God to give them the sevenfold gifts eat His Holy Spirit to carry them through this new warfare. Be im- pressed upon them the importance of at erabing Holy Com- munion often and regularly, and they would thus gain new life and new strength to carry them through this world. Tars CALLING Our OF FHB RESERVBS —The issue of the special circular from the War Office calling out a portion of the First-class Army Reserve, and notifying the probability of a further call upon aro Reserves of ell arms at an early datd, has been provocative of great excitement in the mili- tary centres throughout the United Kingdom. The appear- ance on Wednesday morning of the posters notifying the . calling out of the Reserves on the gales of the various bar- racks led to the gathering of a number of meu who did not even wait for the customary notification to• be delivereil at their residences either by post or by the hands of the local police to present themselves for duty. The net strength of thelqrst-class Army Reserve on the tat January, 18S5, was 39,244 men, consisting of 1,036 cavalry 1,692 artillery, 655 engineers, 331610 infantry, 833 Com- missariat and Transport Corps, and4ls7 Medical Stiff Corps. The increase during the year 1884 amounted to 4,655 of all arms. From an early hour on Wednesday morning the Horse Guards was thronged with officers des.rens of active employment in the event of hostilities breaking out. ;For some time past every arrangement has been made for the immediate embodiment and despatch of an Army Corps at the shortest notice to any point required. Such an army corps would comprise elle regiments nf cavalry, 21 battalions of infantry, four batteries of Royal Horse A,tillery, U. bat- teries of field artillery, three reserve ammunition colcmna, and one ammunition reserve corps. The cavalry would number 3,918 officers and men, with 3,090 horses; the in- fantry 23,037 aficers and men; and the artillery 4,000 officers and men, with 5,676 horses and 90 guns. On Thurs- day a large number of reserve men in Warrington received notice to join their regiment by an early date. There are about 300 reserve rues belonging to the Bth King's •( Liver- pool) Regiment, many of whom live in and about War- rington. The call is being eagerly responded to. SELECTION OF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR THE ATXRIN- CRAM DIVISION.—A large and influential meeting of repro- sentatives from the whole of the district comprised in the newly-constituted divisien of Altrincham, which extends from Lymm to Stockport, was held in the lecture hallo( the Altrincharn Reform Club, on Saturday, for the purpose of accepting theiecommendations of the Provisional Commit- tee held last month for the election if members to the ex- ecutive council, for the election of officers, and the selection of a Liberal eandidate for the division. The president of the new Parliamentary division, Mr Joseph Leigh, of Stock- port, presided.—On the motion of Mr David Senior, of Bow- don, seconded by Mr Albeit Nicholson, of Sale a number of gentlemen were appointed vice-presidents of the association, and additions were made to the Executive Corn mittee.—Mr 'William Milne, in proposing Mr Isaac Saunders Leadain, M.A as the Liberal candidate for that division paid a graceful ' compliment to their political veteran, Mr Latham, who bad so ably contested the Mid-Cheshire division in the Liberal interest. Mr Milne enlarged at length upon the special qualifications of Mr Leaden,' who, he said, was an active and earnest member of the Farmers' Alliance, he was a great authority on commerciii as well as agricultural questions, a sound Liberal, a winning and impressive sfreaker, a willing and arduoua worker, and was intellectually and by cultivation and social standing eminently qualified to represent that division in the Hotels of Commons. (Ap- plause.)—Mr Swanwick seconded the nomination, and ro- marked that Mr Leadatn would thoroughly combine the various sections of the party. (Hear, hear.)—Mr George Hooke and the Chairman supported the motion, which was carried unanimously and enthusiastically.—Mr Leadarn, on Monday, accepted the invitation to contest the Altrincham division of Cheshire in the Liberal interest. Mr Leaiam and Mr Rigby were the accepted Liberal candidates for Mid- Cheshire before the proposed alterations in the county divi- sions were effected.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER:
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER:
LONDOn THURSDAY, An interchange of diplomatic notes is KM passing be.

tween London and St. Petersburg ;'and still goes forward throughout Russia, and all over the empire on which the sun never sets, the task of arming. Day by day reports 1 vary as to the probable issue. One afternoon the air is balk of assurance of peace, and in the morning we wake up to find the almost certainty of war. This morning it is ware . and, Rea particular report be true, the stout assurance of seine who have always prophesied peace must give way. The statement is that the Russian government declines to institute further inquiry into the Penjdeh affair, not admit. ting that any doubt attaches to General Komaroff's state. ment. If that be so, it is equivalent to a declaration of war. It seems incredible, but it receives confirmation from a let- ter also published this morning, which purports to be the answer of M. de Giera to the request of the British govern- ment for an explanation of General Komoroff's conduct. The Russian Minister not only declares that General Ko- maroff's despatch contains the desired explanation as to the events at Penjdele, but that the Russian Government have nothing to add to it. Of the right of the Russian Government to make the statement I have nothing to say. If we turn about the figures in the drama and suppese that it is Russia asking us to disavow some particular action of General Lumsden of which that officer gave a version justifying his conduct, we should see that it is not, after all, so monstrous a thing for a Government to stand by its own officials. The impore tance of this sta'ement, assuming it to be authentic, is that it closes the door against a pacific settlement. It is true that at the cicso of this same despatch M. de Giers expres- ses the hope that the Penjdeh incident shall not prejudice the continuation of those negotiations which aim at streng- thening the good relations between the two Empires. But in this connection these are empty words. lithe version of GeneraeLumaden be a correct one, the attack on Penjdeh was a deliberate act of agreasion wantonly taken in defiance of a diplomatic eiteation very recently strengthened by a specific declaration that no adv.nca should be made en either side. The British Government have accepted General Lumsden's etatemect. and unless this country is prepared to receives slap in the face publicly administered, where not only Europe but India and Asia might witnes4 it, RDPBiil man dieavove the action of General Komar( !. 'lassie, it is said to-day, declines to disevow I', arga!, there will be war. The demand for a vote of credit of £11.000,000 is the first stoke in the impending conflict, and upon it England may be said to have scored heavily. It must make the mouth of the Czar'a ministers water to think bow Mr Glad- stone can come down to the House of Commons, ask for eleven millions sterling, and have the demand heartily met with offers of as mach more as may be needed. Russia, It is said, has recently been making desperate efforts to rake at ruinous interest a miserable couple of millicns, which would be a mere bucketful in the ocean of expenditure upon which she seems Inclined to embark. This is the point of view from which war with Russia, if war there must be, may be regarded, not boastfully, but without apprehension. Such a war would be one of the most calamitous misfor- tunes that has befallen thiscountry. It is not only the cost of it in the way of taxation that will impoverish England. There is the inevitable check to trade. That means percep- tible loss to the average father of a family who works in the honourable obecurity of the city or the shop. Such a lwar, which able editors discuss as a grand abstactine from which only glory can scintillate, will come home per- sonally to innumerable households. To some it will leave for ever vacant chairs and saddened hearts. In all, it will directly or indirectly reduce the income. But where Eng- land will have its ever-growing prosperity checked, Buena will be simply and irretrievably ruined. Where she gets the money from to move forward her armies and prepare her fleet now is a mystery. Where she will get it six months hence with war encircling her ports with an impassable flame of fire is a question not difficult to answer. She will not be able to get it at all, except in such a measure as it may be wrung out of an already over-taxed people. There was one portion of Mr Gladstone's statement when moving the Vete of Credit on Tuesday that went along way towards reconciling people to this demand. Of the £11,000,000, four avid a half is on account of the Soudan. But it is to bs applied to the winding-up of that unhappy business. I have several times ventured to predict that the march to Khartoum would never take place, and that be- fore the full heals of summer fall upon the British camp the tents would be deserted. It is nevertheless pleasing and satisfactory to have the forecast officially carfirined. The seasoned army, 30,000 strong, now pining in the Sou- dan, will be drafted to India should war break out with Russia. In the happier alternative they will come home. Thus good arises out of evil. lied the attention nf the Con- servatives been concentrated upon Egypt they would have made it exceedingly difficult for tire Government to take this step. Tee opportunity of distraction has been boldly and adroitly seized, and at least our necks will henceforward be free of the Soudan millstone.

The street of the crisis has acted upon the Poet Laureates and, like Mr Silas Wegg, he has dropped into verse, for his greatest admirers, among whom I count myself, can scarcely rail his latest lucubration poetry. It Comes nearer to his famous outburst of some years ago, beginning ". I stood ma a tower In tbe wet." I wonder what Alfred Tennyaon would have said thirty years ago, supposing someone had asmred him that the day would come when he would write a line like this and call it poetry '‘ This tale, the mightiest naval power on earth." Even M. Jourdain, if he had spoken this use, would at Once have recognised it as prose. Lord Beaconsfield's admirers, who have crowned with primroses his statue in Parliiment-iquare. meant well. But they cannot be congratulated upon the spectacular result of the demonstration. Even when the primroses were fresh the arrangement had a ludicrous effect. One elaborate con- trivauce, several feet square, was composed of a groundwork of primroses, with a centre of violets forming the letters of the famous phrase "Peace with honour." As the tender primroses have laded in the London atmosphere, this thing has more and more assumed the appearance of a door mat. A wreath placed on the head and dependent from the neck looks like a lamentable old rope, whilst the innumerable bouquets tossed over the railings, lie at the foot of the statue a mass of corruption. One obscure person, anxious to asso- ciate his name with that of a great stateseaao, sent a wreath with a huge visiting card in which the name of "our beloved and regretted Premier, the Right Honourable the Earl of Beaconstied, K.G." is shrewly linked wi.h that of the ob- scurity, whose game I for one will not play by spelling it om. This person, varying from the poet laureat., tags ty simple expeti:.:::. turned a line of prose into Terse. ~Tho' defeated or n 0 o'er again, ha was ns'et di9graced." is given as a quotation :row:. Times article. On the whole the best thing any friend of Loru Zasconsfiel I can do is to take broom and bucket and nail awoy the melancholy rubbish through which the figure of the late !wemier sar- donically smiles. Many people will probably share the surprise with whic:. I learned the other day that Mr Bright never, or hardly ever, reads Shakespere. When we come to think of it the great orator, prone to adorn his speech with quotations. from the poets, rarely goes to Shakespero for assistance. The ebjection Mr Bright takes, and with characteristic frankness admits, is that he cannot enjoy the dramatic term of the poetry. His special favourite is Milton, from whom he frequently quotes. Perhaps next in his estimation, though coming a long way off, is Whittier, towards whom ; he is of course attracted by the common bend of religious denomination. But Whittier has for the ordinary reader- much beyond his Quakerism to recommend him, being one of the tenderest singers of modern times. It is, I think, in. the Congregational Hymn Book that worshippers in English chapels entertain Whittier unawares. There is an American poet of quite another character whom Mr Bright adrnlres, and did much to introduce to English readers. This is Mr Ruasell Lowell, from whose " Biglow papers" he once quoted with the effect of sending eve:yona in search of the volume itself.

11 Mr Irving, returning from America, has taken lints front managers as American actors have taken hints from him. He is going to make his pit and his gallery all to consist ef reserved seats. It will need a very little outlay, but the gain to the public will be great. No doubt all tile other managers will follow the lead. The eingular thlig is that so sensible and simple an innovation should Lane been so long delayed. It has been in use for years in all the German and Austrian theatres, and even in the Grand Opera in Paris yoa can take reserved seats in the top gal- lery, though there you are charged heavily for bickina. I do not think 'Mr Irving proposes to give his sr,u,ry choice of seats, but he will adopt a system first introduced into London by Mr Wilson Barrett. Every seat in the theatre will be represented by a little slip of card like a rail- way ticket, and these are what will be sold. Tt•ere will be ne hocking, the ticket will be handed to the purchaser, and S 5 there will be no duplicate of it there will be no mistake possible. •

We pictures were very unequal—aome of them, especially the Spanish subjects, have reached the magic fan of four figures, but he painted too many pot boilers to commanl a high, price in the market--unless for exceptional excellence. Da- ring the early part of his career Landscer was a lion in hie path, and on the death of Landseer the new school, with Peter Graham and Davis, soon came to the front and kept . is. He had a very interesting studio next ElcuVrea its South Kensington.
On Thursday the brigantine Cbarles George, of C, wee, col- lided with a large steamer off Beachy Head. The former sank, and the master and mate were drowned.

AN ARRANT KNAVIL—Thomas Harris, a surveyor, was sentenced at the South Wales Assizes, on Thursday, to five years' penal servitude on pleading guilty tn several charges of forgery, fraud, and embezzlement. The nrisoner, who was deacon of a chapel, had obtained about £30,000 from building societies, public bodies, Welsh Methodist ministers, • and many poor people by a series of what Mr Just;ce Field described as "unblushing forgeries, committed under the cloak of religion."

She has been frequently sent toe gaol for a month without tha cption of a fine.

WZDNESDAY.—Before Mr F H Gossaga and Mr H Gasket], junr. liltscurxenscrus.—John Byrne, an elderly man, pleaded guilty to begging in Birchtieul lane en the previous after- noon, and he was sentenced to seven diys' hard labour.-- Patrick Concannon, Ellen Quinn, Ann Martin, John Glr.v.*, Inkermann Lee, Thomas Roberts, and John Wrltugh were each fined 5a and costa for oh unkenness, TRANFERS.—The IiCoD9O Of the Church Beerhouse, Church-street, Farnworth, was transferred from Thomas Harwell to H E Harrison ; the Wellington Hotel, Preecot. from Edward Bogers to Price Griffiths the Cross Keys Hotel, Appleton, to Mrs Annie Higgins from her late hus- band; the British &Idler, Fccleston, from E B Evans to "'nes Tirer ; the Base and Crown, Huyton, from C J Sorge to Thomas Morris. Caratterry on Fran —Robert Bushill, of Davy-street, was on the evidence of P.C. Cummins fined Is and costs for this

offence. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF FIGS.—Ann Coyle, an elderly woman, was ordered to pay costs 7s 63 for having on the Bth inst. moved two pigs in a Swine fever infected area.— P.C.' s Elsworth and Savary provel that the pigs were in De street.

- _ PRESCOT. COOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Monday, present—Meres W L Evans (in the chair), W Goldsworth, J T Had, J 13 Sanders and II Cross (clerk).— The School Attendance Officer (ir. Bayliss) reported that during the last quarter 40 chilAren reached the age of 5 years, and were attendiog the following schools i—Church Schooll2,Board School 9, Yew Tree School 10, private schools 9.—ln reply tn fhe Chairman, Mr Bayliss said the epidemic of measles had somewhat ceased, nod several chil- dren who had been absent had got tack to school.—Mr Ellison, one of the assistr.nt masters at the boys' school, sent in his resignation because the Board bad taken from him the privilege to administer at his discretion corporal pun- ishment to refractory scholars. The Board decided to ac- cept the resignation.—lt was decided to increase the salary Of miss Sayer, assistant mistress of the Ririe school, front £4O to £45 per year. After some discussion it was decided that the " call " for the ensiling half year should be £250. The monthly return of attendances daring March as com- pared with the corrcspondisg month last year was presented. This was the only business of importance.

SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT SUTTON. NEAR ST. HELENS. —About eleven o'clock on Thursday forenoon the district of Sutton was thrown into a state of great excitement by a rumour that Mrs Hamiltsn, wife of James Hamilton, labourer at Sutton Glass Works, and formerly gardener to Mr William Blinkhorn, J P., had drowned one of her four children and committed suicide in the same way, in the small but deep reservoir attached to the Sutton Glass Works. It appears that about 10-30 Mrs Hamilton was seen by a Mrs Marsh goin.; towards Brooklands Bridge with her son Thomas, aged four years. A little while afterwards Mrs Marsh returned, and saw Mrs Hamilton lean- ing over the railing of the bridge. She passed ?DI but immediately afterwards heard screaming, and lack- ing round found that Mrs Hamilton and her child had dis- appeared, and were strtwgling and screaming in the water. An alarm was raised, and the first person to arrive Was a rag-gatherer named Hagan, who got into the water, which was only four feet deep. Lie, however, declined to go farther than up to his knees, and scrne little time elapsed before two other men, namod lia-rlow and Redmond, arrived. Theyimmediately jumped in, and got out the poor woman and child, but life was extinct. The two bodies were re- moved home to Highfield-terrace, Sutton. Mrs Hamilton was 40 years of age. She has lately been in a very low state of mad, and had been heard to say she owed some money, and could not hear to face things. The family had been in better circumetancvs. BRIDAL 130O4LnET BLoon, for beautifying the com- plexion. It imparts exquisite beauty to the face, neck, arms, and hands. GENEPAL

- - The lighthouse at Cape Ray, Newfoundland, Las been destroyed by fire. Dr Blakerley, Dean of Lirceln, died at his residence in Lincoln on Saturday morning. Twelve hundred miners, out on strike, paraded the streets of Sheffield on Monday, headed by a brass band, in order to excite sympathy and obtain support. It is announced that the Great Northern Railway Com- pany are about to abolish the second-class carriages running on all but their main and metropolitian lines. During a fire which occurred on Sunday night at a farm in Perthahire fifty cattle and a number of pigs and poultry were burned to death. A large stock of grain and hay was also destroyed. The Glasgow Town Council have awarded gold medals to Chief Constable M'Call and Supts. Boyd and Donald for their clever apprehension of the ten derearnitards convicted of ex- ploding the Glasgow gasometer. EAIBEZZLSMENT OF £9so—At the Jedburgh Circuit Court, on -Tuesday, Thomas Henderson late teller in the Bank of Scotland. pleaded guilty to embezzling £950. He was sentenced to fifteen months' imprisonment. For placing stones and other dangerous obstructions on the Midland Railway line near Harpenden, and thereby en- dangering the safety of passengers, George Barton was sen- tenced at the Hereford Assizes on Wednesday to fifteen years' penal servitude. &footmen BICYCLE ACCIDENT.—At the Isle of Man on Saturday a young man named Fisher, aged 19 years. was riding to Douglas on a bice cle to play in a football match. When apnroaching the foot of a bill in Santon be WAS thrown off and was picked up dead, his neck having been broken. Arthur Cele. a private in the 16th Lancers, is in custody at Liverpool charged with stealing jewellery to the value of £1,400 from Ca wain Crawford, whose servant he was. The prisoner stole the valuables during his master's absence, and absconded, but was arrested when landing from the Dublin steamer. DrATII OF MR. R. ANiDELL, R A —The death is an- nounced at the age of 70, of Mr B. Ansdell, RA, who in some respects was considered to be as great a painter as Sir E Landieer, though there Was not in his pictures that Pathetic interest which characterised the productions of the painter of "The Shepherd's Chief Mourner." The proposal of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company to shorten their line from a point near le irkbain so as to relieve the Bleckpool excursion traffic was on Wed- nesday rejected by the House of Commons Select Commit- tee, it being considered that the projected line would inter- fere unnecessarily with the highroads and drainage. SAD RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—On Situday. George Bares. ford, engine fireman, bad both legs taken off above the knee by the engine of a goods train, which knocked him down as he was crossing the line at Heaton Mersey siding. He was taken to the Stockport Intionary on a stretcher, and is now in a most precaricus condition. He had only been married two months. DESTRUCTIVE FlRE.—Early on Thursday morning a destructive fire broke out at Pantyocloin, near Wrexham. Before it was extinguished it had destroyed a block of buildings and burned 14 head of cattle and three horses. The Wrexham Velunteer Fire Brigade were soon or the spot, and rendered valuable aseisatnee. The buildings and stock are at least partially insured. TEE SCCI;L SCIENCE CONGRESS AND THE GENERAL Eaacrtox.—The Council of the Social Science Ace )ciation have passed a resolution to the effect that in the prospect of. a general election in November it is undesirable to hold al congress this year. They have therefore declined the invi- tation from Bath to meet there in the forthcoming autumn, but they have expreseed a hope that the invitation from that city may be renewed for the year 1886. TEE COST OF THE ARMIES OF EUROPE —For the seventeen States of Europe the total of the armies en a peace footing is 2,529,522 men. Calculating their wages at 2s 6d per day, and omitting the holidays, we have a sum of X.:37 10s per annum for each man. Multiplying this sum by 2,529.522, the total comes to £94.820 575 per annum. Adding to this the total of the 17 war Budgets,which is £101,672,782, the total loss suffered annually on account of her armies is 196,514,852 TRAGEDY ON BOARD SHIP.—The three members of the crew of the barque Wellington who were charged with kill- ing Captain Armstrong during a desperate struggle on board that vessel when off Plymouth were indicted on Monday at Devon assizes. It was shown that the captain bad indis- criminately fired upon the crew with a revolver, and re- ceived his fatal injuries during the attempt to disarm him. Mr Justice Hawkins directed the jury to acquit the pri- soners, and they were released. Sorg AND BONES.—On Monday, at Moss, Denbighshile, an irquiry was opened into the cause of death of Mary Jones, 12 years of age. The deceased and six other children were deserted by their mother on the 11th inst, and have been so neglected by their father that the deceased, whose body was a mere "bag of skin and bones," died while sit- ting in a chair on the lath. Some of the bones were pro- truding through the skin. The inquiry was according ad- journed to the 27th inst. INDIA'S LOYALTY.—The Marquis of Ripon, speaking in reply Co the toast of "Our Indian Empire," at the house dinner of the London City Liberal Club, on Tuesday night, said he had not abandoned all hope of a peaceful solution of the present difficulty between England and Russia, consistent with our national honour and the engagements of the Crown. Should war break out, however, be was certain of the loyalty of the Indian people to England, and it had been one of the springs of his Viceregal policy to strengthen the attachment of the native porSulation to their Sovereign. MawerrEstren ASSIZES —At the Manchester Assizes on Wednesday the three men, Simpson, Lord, and Blackhouse, who were found guilty on Tuesday of committing a series of burglaries in the suburbs of Preston, were celled up for sentence. Blackhouse, it will be remembered, was also convicted of severely wounding two police constables named Smirk and Wilkinson. Blackhouse was sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude, Lord to ten years' penal ser- vitude, and Simpson to twelve months' imprisonment with hard labour. For the manslaughter of her father at Bolton, on the 29th November last, after receiving great provoca- tion, Mary Ryan WAS ordered to be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for six months. MURDER AND SUICIDE.—On Wednesday. a man named Head, who lived with his wife at 40, Marshall-street, Golden Square, London, murdered his wife and then committed suicide. The man Was a coachman, and was understood to be on good terms with his wife. The frost room of the house is occupied by their married daughter, whose hus- band was startled abont half-pest six on Wednesday morn- ing by a scream proceeding from the back room. He imme- diately went to see what the cause was, but fouua the door locked. This he eventually forced. to nod his mother-in- law lying in bed with her %wog cut from ear to ear, while his father-in-law was standing by wills a knife in his hand, vitas 'ditch he had succeeded in gashing his own throat. Dr. Corrie Grant, who visited the place, found the woman quite dead, and the man dying and quite enable to speak. He expired shortly afterwards. Head had been out of work for about 18 months, but had recently obtained employment. It is asserted that there is lunacy in the family, one son, aged 21, being at present in an asylum, while the youngest child, aged 14, is an imbecile. Head was rather over 50 years of age, his wife heing rather younger. The room occupied by the deceased was comfortably furnished, and they were not in absolute want. TEE LONDON DYNAMITE Ongnasiss.—At the opening of the session of the Central Criminal Court, London on Mon- day, the Recorder, in charging the grand jury, said the two men Cunniegbam and Burton' who are now awaiting trial were prosecuted under the Treason-Felony Act. They were cha-ged that together with divers persons unknown, , they d' 1 conspire to deprive the Queen of the Imperial 1 Crown, and by force to compel her Majesty to alter her policy and course, so far as her Ministers were concerned, and to upset the Constitution of the country. There was' no doubt that if these two men used dynamite for the pur- pose of producing a general terror in this country, 80 as to affect the government of Ireland, they would come within the scope of the Act. The grand jury would find a strong prima facie cise against the prisoners, and he thought they would have no difficulty in finding a true bill. The grand jury on Tuesday returned a true bill against the two alleged dynamitards Burton and Cunningham, tor treason- felony. They at the Same time made a statement compli- menting Inspector Ebberline and the other police afficers engaged in the carte. Last Wednesday Mr Justice Hawkins heard as application to postpone the trial of Cunningham and Burton, who are indict.d in connection with the recent dynamite outrages. The application was on .the ground that important witnesses still in America would be called to prove an alibi. The Judge fixed trial for the 11th of May. LORD SALISBURY IN Weans —Lord Salisbury opened the Conservative Club at Wrexham on Tuesday evening, and afterwards addressed a large public meeting. He criticised the foreign policy of the Crevernment, which, he said, had blundered and bungled the policy of the late Ministry in Ezypt. As to the Russian advance in Afghanistan, he con- tended it was impossible in the face of experience to trust Russian assurances. The mode of dealing with Russia was not to exact promises which she would not keep. The heel- tating policy of the Government arose from conflicting elements in the Cabinet. What they wanted was clearness of purpose, and resolution to carry the purpose out. As to the accusation of want of policy on the part of the Conservatives, he said with respect to details in opposition they had no policy ; it was not their business to furnish the Government with a policy upon which to draw their bells and write their despatches. Lord Salisbury concluded his visit to Wales on Wednesday, and addresse4 a large meeting at Welshpool, under the pre- sidency of the Earl of PoWis. Lord Salisbury referred to the grave circumstances under which they bad met ; but said, whilst affording the Government support, the errors committed must be pointed out. Ha described the present Micistry as incompetent, area said had Lord Beaconsfield s policy been followed up the sicr,fice of- life which had been witnessed would never have occurred. In the midst ;of de- pression we remained the solitary example of Free Trade, and although we could not return to Protection, we could not overlook the stolid and apathetic way in which the Government treated any desire for inquiry. There was a lurking doubt, a want of stability, and uncertainty, and those who had capital would not invest. Therefore it be- hoved us more than ever to look to cur colonies; and if the Empire were in danger at all, it was because it hod been shackled ard coerced by men like Mr Bright and Sir W Lawson. The policy pursued had led to a system of hoard- ing, which had mischievously marked Countries where revo- lutionary measures were threatened.
