div.head: TEE EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL 25, 1885.
div.p: TEE EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL 25, 1885.

1 and J Inglis, shipbuilders. of Glasgow, said that vessels could easily be furnished with lidded masts. He found that about DO per cent, of the tonnage of the country could easily ' use the canal.—Captain Pearson, marine surveyor and nautical assessor, Liverpool, said he had a practical know- ledge of all matters connected with shipping. The Runcorn Bridge would offer no practical impediment to the ship canal. The bridge left a clear headway of 75 feet at high tide, and 70 feet only was required. There was difficulty in docking vessels at Liverpool owing to the exposed posi- tion of the north docks.—Mr Warton, cattle dealer, of Man- chester, said the canal would enable cattle dealers in Man- chester to save 2s per bead on the carriage of cattle, and Od per bead on sheep —Mr Hudson, provision factor, of Man- chester, said the imports of Cork butter to Liverpool from May to October were 21,800 fukins, and of that 13,000 firkins were handled by the Manchester dealers.— Mr A B Tott, of Runcorn,shipbroker and canal carrier, said: —The principil imports there were pottery material, china clay, pig-iron slates, &c. ; the principal exports were salt, coal, and pitch. The total seagoing tonnage coming to Runcorn was 230,000 tons a year ; in addition to which there was a large inland traffic over the canal and going down to Liverpool. It would ba greatly to the advantage of Runcorn if the Ship Canal were made. The shipowners of that place were in favour of the scheme.—Cross-examined by Mr Pope : In his opinion the canal could bring trade to Runcorn that did not now exist there.—By Mr Pember : He thought it was sufficient to provide that whenever there was any impediment to the traffic at Runcorn by the canal, then the Runcorn Commissioners should have the free use of the canal.—Mr Henry Boddington, managing director of a brewery in Manchester, said he had subscribed to the pro- motion of the scheme. He intended himself to take £lO,OOO worth of shares in the company.—Mr Price Williams, CE., said :—The altered gradients which the canal would cause in the North-Western lines were not so diffiuclt as in last year's scheme. In the worst case, the lods of time to the fast trains would only be about a mirute.—Mr Pember said this would conclude the eviuence for the promoters.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CINAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CINAL.
MONDAY. - EXAMINATION OF ALDERMAN BURGESS.

The inquiry into the Manchester Ship Canal scheme was continued on Monday in the House of Lords before the Se- lect Comittee, presidtd over by Earl Cowper, and further commercial evidence was taken. After the examination of Mr W U Cornforth, of Manchester, the noble Chairman in- timated that the Committee proposed to insert in the Bill I a clause requiring the promoters to raise half the capital— he would say five million pounds—before the works were commenced. Counsel for the promoters assented, and stated that Mr Pember last year Gffored, on behalf of the promoters, to insert such a clause. Mr J Leigh, cotton spinner, Stock-- port; Mr Alfred Walmsley, Stockport ; Mr J Rawlinson, Secretary of the North and North-East Lancashire Cotton Spinners' Association; Mr S Ogden, manufacturer,Mancher e Mr S Andrew, secretary of the Oldham Master Cotton Spinners' and Manufacturers' Aesociati on, were also examined in support of the scheme. Mr John Burgess was next examined by Mr Balfour Browne.—You are an alderman of the borough of Warring- ton and justice of the peace, and you have been a member of the Town Council, I believe, for the lest 30 years, and you have been twice mayor of the borough? Yes, that is so.—You attend to give evidence here on behalf of the Cor- poration? At the request of the Corporation I appear here to give evidence.—We may say that Warrington is practi- celly unanimous in favour of the ship canal ? That is so. —And has, during this year, become one of the promoters of the Ship Canal Bill ? Y€9.—The number of the rate- payers who voted in favour of the resolution to promote the Bill I should like to give to the Committee through you ? The number of ratepayers who voted for the Bill was 6,355 —that was for aiding in the promotion of the Bill.—And for subscribing to the expenses ? Yes, and for subscribing to the expenses.—How many voted agaiest ? 515 —That makes twelve to one in favour of the apnlicetion of the rates or the purpose of promoting the canal ? Yes, that is so.— I do not know whether this 515 represents opponents of the canal, or merely opponents against applying the rates to the promotion ? Poesibly both—Warrington at the present time has a considerable popul atiou—how many ? About 45,000 people.—What is the principal trade carried on there ? We have a variety of trades in Warrington. Iron and wire work, tanneries of a very extensive character, soap- works, glass work', cotton mills, file mills, and tools. There is a great variety of manufacture Warrington is 181 miles from Liverpool by railway, and 20 miles by river, is it not ? It is more than 20 miles by river.—We know that it is a tidal river up te Warringtoo ? It is a tklal river up to Warrington weir.—At the present time is the river made of much use in carriage between Warrington and Liverpool ? So far as ordinary carrying is , concerned it is not made of much use.—Will you tell the Committee why ? The tides do not admit of that regu. lerity in carrying that will permit it to be used —lt is only at high tides, of course, that the ships can get up ? lit is only at certain tides that the ships can get up —The tide requires to rise 16 test over the Liverpool old dock sill? Yes.—lt would be only seven t'des a fortnieht when vessels get up to Warrington ? Something like that.— What class of vessels got up, ships or barges ? Simply barges of 70 or SO tons.—lt is the proposal of the promo- ters to prcvide 20 acres of the dock for the town of Wae- rington ? Yes.—Do you think that that dock, in conjunc- tion with the works of the canal, will be of great service to the trade of your town? Uequestionably.—l believe you are chairman of the Sanitary Committee of the borough ? Yes.—Has that Committee hid before it very frequently the question of floods ? Yrs.—Do flocde do considerable harm to the town by backing up the sewers and making them difficult to diech arge ? No doubt of I believe you despair of a remedy until the ship cen.l ? Yes, we shall have no remedy, and cannot possibly have unless through that instrumentality.—le that feature, do you think, of the canal scheme an important sanitary one ? It will help us undoubtedly.— Mr Pope states that he has nothing to ask the witness —There is the Runcorn and Latchford Canal belonging to us? Yes.—That obviated, the necessity of using the river ? I speak of those parties who use the tidal river.—When you sty that the river is not much used, you do not mean to say that we, the owners of the river, do not provide you with good means of water communication between Runcorn and Warrington ? Be- tween Runcorn and Warrington by river there is very little traffic, but through your canal there is a deal of traffic You know we are spending a considerable sum of money in improving even the river commuuication ? I shall know it when I see you spend it.—ln other words, you will not be- lieve anything ; you will only believe your eyes? I have known the company too long to allow me to believe much. —You will not believe them if they come and swear that they are doing it? I do not say that.—You will not ex- pect more than you can get? No. Mr Robert Peers, the Mayor of Bury, having given evi- dence in favour of the scheme.—Mr Alderman Husband, of &al ford, was called. He said he attended in pursuance of a resolution passed by the Town Council of that borough, and he regerded the scheme as essential to. the recuperation of the commercial properity of Salford.—The Committee then adjourned.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Mr J W Radcliffe, Ma-y;r-o-f-Old-h.am, and a flannel manu- facturer, carrying on business at Rochdale, said he appeared in his official capacity to give evidence in support of the scheme. One-fifth of the whole cotton imported, or about 110,000 tons a year, was consumed in the Oldham district. They got the cotton almost entirely from Liverpool.—Mr W H Houldsworth, M.P., of the firm of Thomas Houldsworth and Sons, cotton spinners, and a director of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, was next examined, and said he was of opinion that the ship'canal would be a great benefit to the manufacturing districts in diminishing the rates of transit. —Mr Makinson, Mayer of Salford, said that the Corporation of that borough were taking part in promoting the bill.— Alderman Bennett, Manchester, said that if the canal were mails he would order whole cargoes of timber direct to Man- chester for the purposes of his own trade.—Mr J C Fielden, cotton spinner, Culchetb, said he had studied and written upon the foreigh competition as affecting the industries of Lancashire. The present year was the anniversary of the first importation of cotton to Liverpool. Since 1755 the trade had grown till now. Three million bales a year were imported from America. The population of Lancashire was denser than that of any other port of the worli, and its increase was almost identical with the growth of the cotton trade. There had been no petted of depression in the trade so long as the present one, which bad lasted far eight years. The saving to the industries of Lancashire by the canal w.,01d be 21. or 3 millions sterling a year. Lonfou alone would be saved £50,000 a year in the costs of Its cotton goods. In the transit of goods exported from Lancashire there would be a saving of £500,000 a year. The question of transit was the only serious disadvan,age the cotton trade had to contend with. He had no doubt that if the canal were made certain towns would still fret their cotton direct from Liverpool, but the largest market wou'd be at Mansbester.—By the Chairman : Excepting those interes- ted in railways there was only an infinitesimal portion of the population concerned opposed to the scheme.—Mr Bid- der : I understood your Lordships to say that it would be a condition, if you approved of the bill, that £5.000.000 should be raised before the works were started.—Mr Peaffier : That would be a question between the promoters and your Lord- ships. You would not force them to have five millions lying idle at their hankers ? The Chairman : No.—Cross- examined by Mr Bidder : There had bean no attempt as yet to raise the capital for the scheme.—The Chairman : There is no question that they will net be able to raise the money.—The Committee again adjourned. WEDNESDAY.

- The Mayor of Manchester (Mr Alderman Harwood) gave eyidenca of the strength of feeling in Manchester and neigh- bourhood in favour of the Ship Canal schema. A good many industries had left the district, and looking to this fact and the general state of trade the City Counciland the inhabitants generally felt that something must be done if they were to maintain their present pcsition.—Mr W A Nicholls, wholesale fruiterer, Manchester, explained the advantage to the fruit trade of direct water carriage to and from Manchester.—Mr Gustav Behrens, of the firm of Sir Jacob Behrens and Sons, merchants, Manchester and Brad- ford, stated that his firm exported annually about 18,000 packages, including casks, or about 6,000 tons, about three- fourths of which went through ports on the east coast. If the Ship Canal were made a large proportion of these good would go by the canal. —Mr J Liebe)), of the firm of Messrs N P Nathan and Sons, mer- chants, Manchester, gave evidence of a similar character.— Mr George Woods, secretary to the Longford Wire, Iron, and Steel Company, Vs arrington ; Mr T Lord, mayor of Hey- wood ; Mr Alderman Boulton, of Ashton-under-Lsmo •, Mr W Warburton and Mr F Moss, calm merchants; Mr J W Southern, timber merchant •, Mr J E Platt, of the firm of Messrs Platt Brothers, Oldham ; Mr J Priest, carrier ; and Mr W Berrisford, grocer, were also examined -Mr Jacob Bright, M.P ' who was next called, said he did not believe that any scheme for public works had ever baen brought before Parliament from any commbinity where so wide and deep a belief in the necessity of the scheme existed as in this case.—Mr Coldington, M.P., corfirrned Mr Brig,ht's evidence.—Mr R Harrison, fruit and vegetable merchant ; Mr G F S:anley, hon. secretary of the Smithfield Market and Produce Traders' Committee; and Mr J T W Mitchell, chairman of the Wholesale Co-operative Society, also gave evid mce.—After consulting with his collragu,s, the Chair- man said that no evidence that might ba given on behalf of Sir H De Trafford rtuarding the impurity of the water would induce the Committee to reject the bill. THURSDAY.

On Thursday, Mr. Jahn Allison, city survoyor of Man- chester, said there would be no difficulty in carrying goods from the canal srver the system of tramways in the city in specially constructed trucks, and such waggons could carry 10, 15, and 20 tone.—Mr. Henry M`.Niel, iron merchant, Manchester, said that on iron goods ths cilial would result in a s‘ving to manufacturers of from 43 to 53 per too. Cc. tracts were often lost for as I;ttle as three half-pence per ton. —Mr. Richard Hart!ey, of the Silkstone and Dedworth Colliery, said the canal would assist in the development of the extensive coalfials of south and West Yorkshire.—Mr. ederick Edwaids, shipowner, Cardiff, said five of the ships of which he was managing ownsr, traded between New York and Cardiff. In his opinion there would be no extra freight to Manches,er as against Liverpool.— William Henry Rat-burn, of the firm of Raelown Brothers, Glasgow, and president of the Clyde Shipownrs' tion, said his firm's vessels numbered 12, and he would not hesitate to send them up the ship canal. He did not think that the insurance premium would be higher to Manchester than it was to Liverpool —Mr Hutchinson, of the firm or .3" P Hutchinson and Co., shipowners, Glasgow, gave similar evidence.—Mr William INlnmillan, enaitieer to Bleasra- A-

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
SATURDAY.

On Saturday an excursion was made by the Royal Visi- tors down the upper and middle Lakes of Killarney to the cottage of Glena. The sun shone brilliantly as they took their seats in Lord Kenmare's barge. The band of the 20,h , R giment played the musical honours and followed in the ' wake of the royal barge, playing a lively selection of airs, the effect of the water cavalcade being altogether unique and pretty. Luncheon occupied a considerable portion of the afternoon, and in the short siesta which followed, the Princess sat out on the terrace in the sunehine. She in- timated her desire to see an Irish jig danced, and four of the boatmen of Lord Kenmare's barge were found who to some extent were accomplished in the art, and who I danced a vigorous measure to the music of the regimental band. The Royal party set off again in the barge across the lake, winding in and out of the islands of the Lnane to give their Royal Highnesses an opportunity ef seeing the beautiful scenery of this locality. After a six-hours' out- ing, the Prince and Princess drove back to Killarney House, where they arrived about seven o'clock. At Killarney House, in the vanilla., a large dinner party assembled to meet the Prince and Princes. SUNDAY. _ .

Their Royal Highnesses attended service at the Parish Church on Sunday, when the Rev. G. R. Wyen, vicar of Killarney, preached the sermon ; and in the afternoon they again visited:Glena,Ross Castle, O'Sullivan's Cascade, Colleen l 3 awn Rock, and other points of interest.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

On Monday morning, the Prince and Princess of Wales and party returned to Dublin Castle from Killarney. IL iv- ing through the town, they were greeted with every mark of respect, and at the railway station the collected towns- people shouted a hearty farewell, and tendered bouquets to the Princ,ss, one or two individuals only hissing as the train left amidst the strains of "Come back to Erin " from the band of the Lancashire Fusiliers. At Tralee a goodly assemblage on the platform loudly cheered the Prince, and and more bouquets wore handed to his consort. Outside the station, however, a different state of feeling showed itself. Some hundreds of the townspeople, mostly of the I labouring classes, lined the walls bordering the railway and tone streets approaching it, and set up a howl of execration at the Royal train, which was here delayed somewhat for no appreciable reason. The hostile spirit of the Nationalists displayed itself again at Abbeyfeale, where a band blurted forth the strains of " God save Ireland "from amidst a crowd collected in the corner of a field, one man bearing a pole with a black piece of calico attached, while hostile inscrip- tions were held aloft on boards. At Ardah there was a strong hostile element, which swirmed upon the archways, bridges, and the walls by the side of the line. Several of ' them defiantly waved strips of black calico or baize above the beads of the crowd, and called for cheers for Parnell. At Limerick, addresses of welcome were presented, and the Prince, in reply, said he hoped ta renew his atria iintance with the various institutions represented. Nothing but goodwill afterwards accompanied the Royal party on the road to Dublin, which was reached at half-past six. TUESDAY.

At Dublin, on Tuesday morning, about 10,000 Sunday School children of the Irish Protestant Church assembled in the grounds of the Viceregal Lodge, and presented an address to the Princess of Wales, consisting of a beauti- fully-illuminated album, which the Princess received with evident pleasure. The Prince of Wales, Prince Albert Victor, with Lord and Lady Spencer, witnessed the cere- mony, which concluded with the singing of the National Anthem. The Royal Party afterwards attended Panchatown races. .

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The Prince of Wales did not go to Punchestown races on Wednesday owing to the rainfall ; but he inspected a body of the Royal Irish Constabulary in Phcenix Park. The Prince was suffering from a cold, the result of biq exposure to the inclement weather of Tueeday. tis rtoyal Highness was, however, able to be prese”., t.gether with the Princess and their son, at a grand ...a given in the evening by the Citizens' Reception Zommittee. THURSDAY.

Th. departure of the Royal party for Belfast brought to- gether a large assemblage at the Amien-street terminus, Dublin, coon after eleven on Thursday morning. Earl Spencer arrived on horseback, and was received with cheers. Amongst others present were Mr Martin, chairman of the Cit,z,..ne' Committee, Mr Guinness, high sheriff of the county, the Chairman and several Directors of Railway Companies, Sir T Steele, Commander of the Forces, General Lord Clarina, Colonel Deese, Hon. Mr Lambton, R.N., Sir Robert Hamilton, Under Secretary, Colonel Bruce, Inspec- tor General of the Irish Constabulary. At half-past eleven the Royal party arrived in an open carriage, and were greeted with hearty cheers. Directly they alighted, Miss Hutton, daughter of one of the railway directors, presented the Princess of Wales with a bouquet. Their Royal High- nesses shook hands with several members of the reception party, and the train left amid cheers, the band of the Corn- wall Light Infantry, which regiment furnished the guard of honour, playing the National Anthem. On leaving the ter- minus, Lora Spencer was loudly cheered, and the assembled crowd waved th,ir handkerchiefs. After passing Drogheda the Royal party received an enthusiastic welcome, which increased as they neared the capital of Ulster. At Porta- down there was an extraordinary crowd assembled in a field adjoining the railway station, and when the train stopped they clambsred up the embankment and filled the station, cheering enthus'astically. At Lisburn, Lurgan, and other stations on the route these manifestations were repeated, and culminated when -the train reached Belfast. Here the streets had been gaily and profusely decorated in honour of the occasion, the result being a dazzling and unique dis- play of colour. Thirty addresses were presented at Ulster Hall to the Prince, who replied, expressing his pleasure at visiting so important a centre of indnstry, and at witnessing the loyalty and devotion of the people tO the Constitution. The Royal visitors drove through the densely thronged streets amid a some of much enthusiasm, and embarked on the R. yal yacht Osborne for Carrickfergus Roads, where she moored for the night.

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HoPu SOCIRTF.—A fairly-attendecl,j meeting in connection with the junior division of this Band of Hope was held in the Brunswick Wesleyan school- room, Cross-lane, on Thursday evening. Mr. A. W. Ken- yon presided, and addresses were given by Mr. Wm. Clare and Mr. J. H. Jones. A meeting of tho senior division was afterw trds bell under the presidenev of Mr. 0. Pickett. The meeting bad been called to consider the advisability of having a piemic in connection with the society during the ensuing summer. The question was ultimately post- poned. MARRIAGE Al TILE WESLEYAN CISAFEL.-011 Thurs- day forenoon at the Brunswick Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Cross-lane, Mr Josiah Cuthbert Atkinson, eon of the late Joseph Atkinson, of Earlettown, was married to Miss Louisa Roberts, eldest daughter of Mr John Roberts, Queen- Street, Earlestown. As both parties are members of the choir at the Wesleyan Chapel and active workers in con- nection with the Sunday school there was a large gather- ing of friends at the chine'. The body of the sacred edifice was crowded. The nuptial ceremony was performed by the Rev J M Fairbourn ; and the happy pair subsequently left Earleslwa for London, where the honeymoon will be spent. NEWTON FOOTBALL Cura.—The annual dinner in connection whit the Newton Football Club was held at the Legit Arms Hotel, Newton, on Satu-day evening. There was a large attendance of members and friends. Mr G Lane (captain of the club) presided and among those present were Messrs T Fairclough, T Egan, Rimtner, T Egan, junr., Hudson, Woods, Derkin, F T Parry (hon. secretary, West Lancashire Union), Critehley, dec. After the usual loyal toasts had been honoured, the Chairman gave " Sac- ems to the Newton Football Club, which was drunk with en- thusiasni.—Mr TFairclough responded, and read the results of the past season. The first team had played 15 matches, 10 beim- won, 3 lost, and 2 drawn, and scored 10 goals, 20 trite, and 61 minor points to opponents 4 goals, 9 tries, and 31 minor points.—The Chairman then proposed "Success to the West Laocashire and Border roans Union," coupled with the name of the bon secretary, Er FT Parry, which was received with musical honours.--Ale Parry, responding, thanked 'hem for the unauimons nvtnnee in which they had received the toast, and sod the Union would do its utmost to foster the Rugby game, and he trusted that Newton, as well as all clubs connected with the Union, would endeavour to play a gentlemanly game.—Songs, &c, were ably ren d . and a pleasant and enjoyable evening was Spent

EARLESTOWNBAPrisr CHAPEL.—During the present week a series of special evangelistic services have been held in the Baptist Chapel, Earlestown. On Monday evening the service was conducted by the Rev W C Tayler (pastor) and Mr G F Aveline, on Tuesday evening by Mr Alexander Pitt (Liverpool), on Wednesday evening by the Rev ti Green, of St Helens, and on Thursday even- ing by Mr Pitt, of Liverpool. On the whole the services have been well attended. ard of an encouraging character. FIBE AT THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHArEL —On Tuesday evening, between half-past six and seven o'clock, an outbreak of fire occurred at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legivetreet. Fortunately t.e3 flames were discov- ered at an early stage and quickly suppressed, or the conse- quences might have, been of a disastrous character. Pre- paratory to the usaal Tuesday evesing's service a fire had been lighted in the vestry of the chapel early in the even- ing. At the time stated aMr John Sephton entered the vestry, which he found nearly filled with smoke, and he ascertained that a quantity of shavings, &c., under the stairs leading to the singers' gallery had caught fire. He secured I • assistance, and the flames were extinguished with buckets of water before any damage to the structure had been done. The plastered walls and oeilieg of the " recess "in which the shavings were stored no doubt prevented the fiances spreading. ALLEGED FORGERY AT FAELBSTOWN FOsT OFFICE.— A case of considerable local interest was heard at the Man- chester Ass,ses on Saturday, when Edward Joseph Banks, 22, clerk, was charged with stealing a letter containing a post-office order for £4 8s 9d ; and also with forging the !signature to the order. It appeared that on Fliday the , 9tb January a post-effics order for £4 83 9d was despatched by Me-srs Hicks, Hargreaves, and Co, engineers Bolton, to one of their employ6s named John Reekie, who was doing work for the firm at Eerlestown. The letter containing the lorder ought to have been delivered to Reekie on the follow- leg day, but although the advice note was received at the Earlestown post-office when Reekie called for his letter at about eight o'clock in the morning, it had not arrived. At one o'clock the same day a young man—who was alleged by the prosecution to be the prisoner—called at the Earles- town office and presented the order for payment. He stated that be had been sent from Bolton to receive the money. The order was *signed "John Reekie," and the prisoner gave the name.of the sender and received the money. The post sffice Officials at Earlestown, however, had thek sus- picion aroused, and the son of the postmaster, Herbert Birk. head, subsequently went to the Bolton and Manchester post- officks, mad at the latter office he saw the prisoner and identified him as the man who had presented the order for payment. The prisoner was engaged in sorting letters at the Manchester post-office on the night of the 9,1 i January, and he was one of two persons through whose bands the letter containing the stolen order would pass in the ordin- ary course of busines'. The prison.r was charged with stealing the le.ter, but denied that he had EiCllc so, and said he had never been in Earleetown in his life. Both Birkhead and a man engaged at an hotel in Earlestown swore posi- tively to seeing him in Earlestown on the afternoon of the 10th January. Mr Taylor, for the defence, set up an alibi. He called a number of witnesses who all swore positively to seeing the prisoner in Manchester at the time he was alleged to have been in Earlestown.—After hearing Mr West in reply, and a lengthy summing up by the judge, the jury returned a verdict of not guilty.—Mr West said there w is a second case against the prisoner which would be gone into, and the prisoner was thereupon remanded.

SANKEY SUNDAY SCHOOL. PRESENTATION OF PRIZES. A gathering et a very pleasant character was held in the Sankey Sugir Wotks School, on Monday evening, when the prizes gained by the Sunday school children for good conduct, attendance, and lessons during the post year were presented by Mr A D Seton. The entertainment had been arranged by Mr W Thompson, jun , and to that gentleman's exertions its gratifying success is mainly due. Tee pro- gramme was gone through by children connected with the Sunday school, and the excellent manner in which the various pieces were given reflected the greatest credit upon Mr W Thompson, jour, Miss Thompson, Miss Hall (mistress of the day school), and Mr Jesse Millard, by whom they had been carefuLy trained prior to their public appearance. There was a very large attendance, and the Rev Canon Whitley, who presided, was supported on the platform by Mr A &ton, Mr W Thompson, sen, superintendent of the Sunday school. and Mr Harry Thomson. The Chairman opened the meeting with a brief address, after which the children sang " The happy little river." " The little brown sparrow " was recited by Miss Sarah A Aspinall, after which a quartette, " Dolly's lullaby," was slang by Mimes Alice Wrigley, Kate Kenyon, Ada Large, and Annie Pill. As each of these children were only five years of age their efforts, when age is taken into consideration, were very creditable, and met with deserved hearty applause. Aft r Miss Sarah Powell had sung "A. merry gipsy girl," Mr Jesse Millard favoured the company with a humorous song entitled "Complaints." A recitation, "The wreck of the Hesperus," was next given by Master Arthur Millard, and "Will you buy my pretty flowers" was then sung by Miss Annie ; the first part of the programme concludiag with the chorus "O'er the moonlit sea." Mr William Thompson, superintendent of the Sunday school, then read the annual report, giving the names of the scholars to whom prizes were to be awarded, and concluded with instructive remarks on good conduct and discipline. Mr A D Seton was then called upon to distribute the prizes. The follow- ing are the names of the recipients. The first prize in each class being for good conduct, and the remaining prizes for good attendance and lessons :—Girls: let class : let prize Annie Millard, 2nd Sarah Ann Rotiowell, 3rd Isabel] Roth- well. A special prize was also presented to Caroline Bailey, who is leaving the school. Second class: let Eliza Lord, 2nd Elizabeth Lord. 3rd Sarah Powell. Third class: let Sarah Ann Lord, 2nd Rachael Clayton. Fourth class : Ist Ada Large, 2nd Nora Wrigley, 3rd Edith Lord, 4th Alice Wrigley. Boys: Ist class: Ist James 2nd Joseph fluke% 3rd James Tunstall. 2nd class: Ist Arthur Millard, 2nd William Burrows, 3rd Arthur Large. 3rd class: let Samuel Large, 2nd John Powell. 4th claim let Herbert Powell, 2nd Edmund Burrows, 3rd Frederick Large, 4th William Bailey. After presenting the prizer, Mr Beton briefly addressed the meeting. He alluded to the remarks of Mr Thompson concerning discipline, and ex- plained how necessary it was for children to be obedient and wall conducted in a, Sunday school. After a few re- marks from Canon Whitley and Mr Flury Thomson, the school children sang "Autumn winds." Mr John Henry Pill then recited "The village blacksmith." A trio, "'rho -three little fairies," by Misses Elizabeth Lord, Susannah Warburton, and EiiZi Lord was very highly appreciated and heartily applauded. Miss Rose Powell sang "Chil- dren's voices," and the chores "Sweet and law" followed. The recitation. "Be strong to do your duty," was next given by Master William Burrows; and Mr rime Millard effectively sang "The three sailor boys." The children then sang the chorus "All among the barley." After a abort Interval a humourons sketch entitled "Shaving done here" was splendidly given by Messrs Charles Millerd, Joseph Tunetall, Jarsee Tunstall, Rishard Swift, William Haseldean, and James Powell. The audielee highly appre- ciated the performance. The proceedings shortly after- wards concluded with cordial votes of thanks to Mr Soon, Mr W Thompson and family, the teachers, and the Chair- man. The meeting throughout had been of a very enjoy- able character.

Warren looked somewhat disetenoortal, but went out of court and quickly came again, and said to Daviaon," When I said I was going to dine with Lord Ly net- hunt, I was joking." " Well " acknowledged Davidson, "so was I!"

- . Two Polish Jews were on a journey one hot summer day. "Have you anything with you, Matthias ?" "Yes, a bottle of Hungarian wine. What have you, Thai ?" "A dry tongue." "Good! Then we'll divide our previsions." "Very good. Begin." Matthias produced a bottle of wine from his wallet, and its contents were honourably divided. After this had been done, Matthias, wiping his month, asked his fellow-traveller to bring out his provision. • I?" answered Tiloff. "Why, yes, your dry bongae !" "I haven't one now r was the reply. A farmer's boy in Scotland was brought up charged with pushing a girl into a mill-pont. In pleading his ease he 11 said he did not push her in—he was only "genii to art ;" whereupon the bailie summarily Informed him that " do't 1 and gaun to do't" were all the same, aad that he would have to pay a fine of ten shillings, or go for ten days to gaol. 11 The boy, not having the necessary wherewithal, was allowed 1 to go and get it from a friend. lii a little while he was again seen standing in court, when the bailie asked if he had paid his fine yet. "No," said he; "but I was gaaa t. do't, ii', as ye say • do't and gaun to do't' are a' the Name, I'm thinkia you an' me 'ill be clear noo!" Not long ago a sloop was loading potatoes at Invergordon. A cart from the country came alongside of her, and the driver proceeded to empty his load into the vessel's hold. When he had finished, he was accosted by the mate, and in- vited to warm and dry himself at the galley-lre, for the morning was wet and stormy and he had a good many miles to go ere he reached home. After a while, the mate gave the man a piece of pork and a ship's biscuit, the latter as hard as a flint. The driver ate the pork with a relish, with- out touching the biscuit. When he had finished, he handed back the indigestible biscuit to the mate, with the remark, ",Here, sailor-man, many thanks; and there's your plate!" It is well known that Thomas Carlyle hated the City. One day business induced him to enter its precincts. Wishing to be informed as to a certain locality of the whereabouts of which he had no notion, he stopped a young man in the neighbourhood of the Bank and asked of him the direction. The young man, recognising his interlocutor, at once volun- teered to accompany him to the required spot. On the way Carlyle opened a conversation with the young man, and elicited from him the fact that he was a clerk ha a City house at a weekly salary. Arriving at their journey's end, Carlyle turned to his guide with a "Now, young man, you may go." "Thank you," said the clerk, by way of a gentle reminder. "Thank you for what?" asked the sage. "Young man," said he, with emphasis, "honesty is the pivot on which the actions of man should hang. You have stolen your employer's time, and now you COINS and ask me to thank you for having done so. The receiver is worse than the thief. Get to your work!" RKCHIPT NOR COOKING EILTSDA.NDS.—MiSEI Carson said at the cooking school yesterday that a Baltimore lady had written a receipt for "cooking husbands so as to make them tender and good." It is as follows: "A good many hus- bands are utterly spoiled by mismanagement. Seine women go about as if their husbands were bladders, and blow them up. Others keep them constantly in hot water; others let them freeze by their carelessness and indifference. Some keep them in pickle all their lives. It cannot be supposed that any husband will be tender and good, managed in this way; but they are really delicious when properly treated. In selecting your husband you should not be guided by the silvery appearance, as in buying mackerel, nor by the gold tint, as if you wanted salmon. Be sure to select him your- self, as tastes differ. Do not go to market for him as the best are always brought to your door. It is far better to have none unless you will patiently learn how to cook him. A preserving kettle of the finest porcelain is the best; but if you should have nothing but an earthenware pipkin, it will do with care. See that the linen in which you wrap him is nicely washed and mended, with the required number of buttons and string tightly sewed on. Tie him in the kettle byaetrong silkcord called comfortable, as theone called duty is apt to be weak. They are apt to fly out of the kettle and be burned and crusty on the edges, since, like crabs and lob- sters, you have to cook them alive. Make a clear steady fire Out of love, neatness, and cheerfulness. Set him as near this as seems to agree with him. If he sputters and fizzles, • do not be anxious some husbands do this till they are quite ' done Add a little sugar in the form of what confectioners calls kisses; put on no vinegar and pepper on any account. A little spice improves them ; but it must be used with , judgment. Do not stick any sharp instrument in him to see if he is becoming tender. Stir him gently, watching the while lest he lie too flat and close to the kettle and so be- come useless. You cannot fail to know when he is done. If thus entreated, you will find him very digestible, agreeing nicely with you and the children, and will keep as long as you want, unless you become careless and set hint in too cold a place—Baltimore Sun. •

A NEW SHOWER BATH.

"I declare," exclaimed Mrs. donee, as her eyes fell on the combined shower and plunge bath, with stops running up and down its side "for all the world like a cabinet organ," as she expressed it, "that's just the thing! And it's so ornamental too !" she added after gazing at it fondly for a minute or so. "Dearest"—she always called Jones "dearest" en occasions like the present—"do you know it's just what I've been waiting for ever so long?" Then the shopkeeper explained the excellence of the bath in most eloquent terms. y palling the different knobs—" stops" as Mrs. Jones persisted in sailing them—one could have douche, hot shower, cold shower, hot wave,cold wave,hst spray, cold spray, hot plange, and cold plunge. The remaining knob was for the waste pipe. "A sort of priecipal stop," suggested Mrs. Jones, still adhering to her organ simile. "Yes, m'em," replied the shopkeeper politely. Then Mrs. Jones looked it all over again, pulling out first One "stop" and then another. Then she held a whispered eenversation with her lord and master. Jones was inclined to be offish at first, but when Mrs. Janes remarked that it would be just the thing for his rheumatiz Jones surrendered and ordered the thing home. The next day was Sunday, and donee got up to try his new purchase. Having removed his elething, Jones get into the bath tub. If there was any- thing Jones hated it was cold water. Therefore he felt aroand for the "hit wave," bat SW lack would have it he got hold of the "cold shower" stop instead, and down came an avalanche of ice cold water upon his poor shivering body. Jones screamed like a pair of panthers, wakiag Mrs. Jones from her morning nap, and putting her in a frame of mind ' not precisely lamb-lik'e. Jones had the "hot plunge" out and wee ap to his neck in boiling water. Mrs. Jones pushed the stop in, and in order to make things even pulled oat the "hot sheerer," stop which sent a stream of scalding water npon his devoted head, making him scream worse than ever. Mrs. Jones couldn't seem to satisfy him any way. She palled at all the stops in snecession—first the " donehe," then the "hot plange," aid now the "cold shower," then she opined half-a-dozen at a lisle, and finally the whole battery. There is no knowing how the thing would have ended hadn't the water given out just as Jones was in his last gasp. One minute more and Mrs. Jones would have been a widow. When the water had mased to flow Mrs. Jones, with great presence of mind, closed all the stops at once. Mrs. Jones is a great woman in an emergency. She rather prides herself on this virtue. But donee is an in- appreciative brute. The first words he uttered when he had recovered his breath were : " Why in thunder did you not do that before?" Mrs. Jones gave him an injured look, but Jones did net see it. He scrambled out of that bath tub into bed, whece be lay groaning, aid all the time making diabolical faces at the cause of his misery. Mrs. Jones did not teat the bath tub herself. Indeed she hadn't the time. She had all she could de that day and two or three days following to anoint the scalded cuticle of her lord with healing lotions. The first thing Jones put en were hie boots. Then he walked de- liberately over to where his "combined shower and plunge bath" stood and kicked it till he was oat of breath. Then he called for the axe and knocked the thing into kindling wood, stops and all. After that, he perched himself atop of of the ruins, and glared about him with demoniacal glee, and it was a good hoar before he could be indaced to die.' mount and put on his clothes. The next day he sect the wreck to the shopkeeper, with his compliments. It was the most satisfying bath tub he ever had, he said; once using satisfied him for all eternity. Bat there are two words com- pletely tabooed la the Jones's mansion, to wit, "bath tub" and "organ stop." Mrs. Jones would no more think of uttering either the one or the other than she would of saying any one of the horrid words uttered by Jones while in the embrace of t'ut hated" oombined shower and plunge bath."

The prisoner kad paid a large part of her wages for the support of her child, which was three years old at the time of its death, and the Judge remarked that the evidence showed that she was devotedly fond of it. His Lordship said be would cheer- fully forwarel to the Home Secretary the jury's recom- mendation of the prisoner to mercy. THROWING VITRIOL.—A young German girl was indicted at the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday for throwing vitriol on her "sweetheart" The girl had been betrayed and deserted by the prosecutor, and in revenge she threw in his face a quantity of vitriol. He was blinded and terribly disfigured. The jury accepted the girl's plea that she did not intend to injure the proeecutor, and acquitted her.

"MUCH ADO ABOUT NOTHING." Sir,—A little affeir that occurred on Sunday and that may be of some interest to your readers has come under my notice. Recently a branch of the Irish National League bite been formed in Warrington, and one or two members of the borough police force have been in the habit of attending meetings held in connection with it on Sunday afternoons, possibly with an idea of being enlightened, or possibly with a view to see how far some of the speakers would commit themselves in waxing eloquent over Ireland's wrongs and expressing their opinions of a certain illustrious family, a prominent member of which has been on exhibition in the Sister Isle for the last few days. On Sunday, lam told, the police as usual presented themselves at the meeting-room, but were informed that they could not be admitted. They, however, with a dignity born of the conscionsnese of power,. declined to ge away, and entered the room. Whereupon, to quote the irrepressible liner, "some disorder ensued amongst the Nationalists," and a resolution was carried that the members of the force be expelled. Although there were sundry ejaculations of " Chuck 'em put," no one pro- ceeded to put the resolution into effect, and the meeting finally broke up in confusion, no business being transacted or speeches made. Perhaps the matter is too trivial to bother about, but I should rather like to know what right the constables had to insist upon being present at a private meeting, when they had been given to understasd that their room was better than their company. Had the meet- ing been a public one it would have been different. We all value nighly the services of our policemen, but should I for one invite a few friends to spend the evening with me and chat upon politics, I should not desire the company of re- presentatives of the law, unless, indeed, they were amongst the invited. If, as I understand, ihe meeting in question was one of 0 members " of the local branch of the League I think it was really a private one, and that being so I don't sea much difference between the two instences. lam not a Nationalist, not even an Irishman, but I think Irish peo • pie should be treated with as much consideration as anyone else. The matter was, however, "much ado about noth- ing," for had the police remained and the meeting gone on I don't suppose they would have heard anything of which they could complain, and their presence need not have much disturbed the Nationalists.—Yours, dtc., READER.

div.head: ALLEGED ENCLOSURE OF A FOOTPATH
div.p: THE ALLEGED ENCLOSURE OF A FOOTPATH

_ NE AR EARLESTOWN. Sir,—Referring to the encroachment alluded to in my letter, which appeared in your issue of llrh inst ,"Spctator:' in his letter of 14th inst. seems to be in doubt respecting a few point i which he raises, and which, with your permis- sion, Mr. Editor, I will endeavour to answer. Spectator' says "If it can b satisfontorily proved that a public footpath has been stopped by the Earlestown Foot- ball Club, then, I say, by all means let steps be taken to prevent it becoming a permanent stopprge." That it is and has bean used as a public footpath for over 30 years, I can testify to, having used it more or less daring that period; and I find the surveyor said at the last meetibg of the Commissioners that "he had evidence of its being used in 1832." " Spectator " again says, "Is it not a fact that the supposed 'public' footpath is only a right of way for the occupier of the laud ; and does not the footpath pass through a farmyard ?" I admit at present the road on the Crow-lane side is approached by prssing through Clarke's farmyard, but it did not always do so ; it was formerly ap- proached by the road at present existing, which passes the houses occupied on the cue hand by Mr. Worsley, and on the other by Mr. Simms ; and if people chose to divert the road they should not blame the public for the diversion ; restore the road to its original course, and what appears to me to be the obnoxious part of the business will cease, viz, the going through Clarke's farmyard, though on that point I feel convinced if the public were to insist on their strict legal rights, they could claim it by length of usage. " Spectator" asks "Ras it ever been a free and open foot- path to the public? If so, why should the gate at the corner of the Mesnes nearest to the farm always have been kept locked and securely fastened; and why should the notice board, Trespassers will be prosecuted,' have been erected ?" In reply, I say the gate has not always been kept locked, , for I myself du not remember a solitary instance in which I found progress barred by the: gate being locked ; and it would bs an easy matter to fird a number of people who have used it limes out of number, without any difficulty whatever; and if anyone using the road in qoestion was a trespasser, and prosecutable, how is it there has not been a multiplicity of prosecutions, for I am sure there has been ample opportunities for so doing. Can "Spectator " quote a single case? I feel a good deal more might be said on the Subject, but I see it is receiving the attention of the Cornm'ssioners, and I trust will have a sa'isfactory termination. Apologising for taking up so much of your valuable space. —Yours &C., RATEPAYER.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING.

_ Sir,—Allow me to have a word with your whimsical -correspondent. Be seems to have lost his temper. This is by no means strange; teetotal bigots, as a rale, care nothing for the advice of their master, that " a soft answer turneth away wrath." Now, I have to charge your correspondent with resorting to subterfuge ; like the speakers at the meeting, he tries to make it appear that his sole anxiety is to get the publicans a day's rest. He will find on examination that this is the nearest approach possible to "twaddle." There is a deal of false sentiment in this argument. The publican and his winsome barmaid lead a very much easier life than girls do in many other occupations, or than workmen do in any of the mills. For proof of this ask any publican hew many applications he receives from girls for situations, or brewer how many applicants he has for his houses. Now be candid, " Whimsical Wane," and say out plainly that you "want the minority to rule the majority." Because you cannot control your appetite, you are determined the moderator shall not have his gill of beer when and where he thinks fit. Tell the people plainly that you know your churches and chapels are not attended by working-men, but you will bring back the good old days when the beadle perambulated the parish , driving all before him to church. Don't resort to subterfuge my " whimsical " friend, and pretend a love for the publican, whom you know in your heart you detest ; but if you want to help any man to a day's rest, why, de- vote your energies to securing the postman. He is a man who, winter and slimmer, early and late, is compelled by , Christians to introduce secular matter to their notice every Surday morning. Stop passenger trains from running on Sundays., coachmen from driving fat rectors and rich patrons tochurch, hurlers from banding round the wine on &endive ; do all this and then look out for "fresh woods and pastures new." I am quite used to the chases. ot coarseness., and when it is made by a Chriettee, a never venture to discuss further, feeibeee-eore, by experience, that! shall be beaten. But, now, what is my stand on the drink question. Simply this, that the tribunal of public opinion is quite sufficient to drive out the drunkard. Time was when it was considered quite the thing for gentlemen to be hauled from under the table the morning after a dinner party, and a six-bottle man was sought after as an acquisition at the table. Public opinion has altered all this; gentlemen are not supposed to get drunk now. Why not the workinr-men adopt the same course ? A an known to get drunk should he shunned. A publican harbouriog "boozers" should lose his license.and the confirmed drunkard should be treated as a diseased subject. There is a large amount of conservatism, Mr Editor, in my composition, and I cannot see some of the social fea- tures of the past slip away without entering my protest. What more calculated to perpetuate gool fellowship than meeting round the festive board ? Why, as Irving says, "It would do one's heart good to hear on a club night, the shouts of merriment, the snatches of song, and now and then the choral bursts of half-a-clozm discordant voices, as the refrain of the good bishop's song was trolled out— Beck and syde go bare, go bare. Bothfolea,.dhfld gorolde, But telly. God senile thee gocd ale enough Whether It be new or o!de, How much of this merriment would you have, after drink- ing a quart of cold water, or a few bottles of pop, or half-a. dozen cups of dyspeptic tea. or a jugfal of back-aching coffee? Why, none !" There is yet another feature about this Sunday closing i business and it is, I think, the most objectionable, that is, calling the law in to say what a man shall drink, and when he shall drink. It is placing such a restraint on the liberty of the subject, that should it ever become widespread would certainly lead to the mental and physical deteriora- tion of the people. In fact, there is a mischievous tend- ency to depend too much upon the State, and too little upon theindiviinal. This hasr already called into existence the " Liberty and Property Defence League," with whose aims and objects I must say I have no sympathy. The League has issued a pamphlet, to which, sir, you referred in yonr last issue, we itten by Lord Bramwell. This pamphlet on Drink" is certainly worthy a more lengthy and serious attention than it received at your hands. After enumerat- ing its evil qualities when taken in excess, the writer goes on to say :—" Drink ! Yes, I say it is a good tie nig, and I think the world Nv u id act very foolishly if it gave it up. Why, if it can do all the harm I have mentioned? For this reason—that it does an immense deal more good. I say outright that P does a deal more good, because it gives a vast deal of pleasure and enjoytnent to those who take it with good sense and moderation. All the world over, with the ex. ception of the crazy fanatic and impostor Mahomed, where. ever the people have had the rkill to make alcoholic drink, they have made and drunk it. Is it not true that it is a source of great pleasure and enjoyment? See the thorough relish with which a tired man takes his glass of beer, the keen pleasure of the first glass of sherry at dinner to the roan exhausted with brain labour. In place of this we have the teetotaller bawling out " Water is the drink for me." His Lordship deals with the question in a frank and honour- able style. He knows, if anyone does, that drink is a curse when taken in excess, same as anything else is when abneed, Quoting Sir James Paget, he says "1 %maid maintain Chic, and all that can reasonably be deduced from it, namely, that the best and, in proportion to nurnbersT the largest quantity of brain work has been, and still is be- ing, done by the people of those nations in which the use of alcoholic drinks has been and is habitual." Compare the brain work of the drinkers of ''drin'r," the inhabitants of England and Germany, and no doubt it will be found superior to that of any non-alcoholic drinking race. Sa much in favour of beer in itself. Now what right have any two men to debit. me from a glass of beer on Sued iy ? Because, they answer, it com- pels someone else to work on Sundays. Well, this someone else is wilting. " It comes to him a boon and a pleasure." Therefore that is not the reason. It ie not front sympathy with the human race, for the selfiehness of teetceallers is proverbial. IA hat then is it ? Simply a strong tl...eiro to

ALARMING EXPLOSION AT TIE ADMIRALTY OFFICE. THE ASSISTANT SEC RE I'ARY INJURED. ACten minutes to eleven OR Thursday morning an ox- plosion which had all the special characteristics of dynamite took place in the official residence of Lord Northbrook at the Admiralty. Although there is comparatively little structural damage, the outer wall of the building is some- what cracked and splintered, not far from the private door which affords an entry to the house from the Horse Guards Parade. In a room which has its outlook at the spot where the wall shows signs of irjery, a considerable amount of damage is evident, the plaster being torn away and the fur- niture completely wrecked. The "wave 'of the explo- sion seems to have made its way from the window of this room, striking as it went the windows of the dining- now, which are in a diagonal line with the supposed locality of the explosion. The glass of the windows, however, as is usual in the case of dynamite ex- plosions, have nearly all been blown outwards, and thickly bestrews the fringe of the garden which lies in front of the hase. At this point, however, the damage is apparently limited to some two or three score of panes of glass. When the explosion took piece Lord Northbrook was absent from the house, but Lady Emma Baring and other members of the family who were at home, were of course much alarmed, although no ene was injured with the exception of Mr N Swainson, assistant secretary and principal clerk, who was engaged near the scene of the explosion, end who sustained severe lacerations from falling glass. A:though the ex- plosion is generally considered to have been that of dyna- mite, a very small quantity of dynamite must have been used, and the question arises, how it could have been introduced into that portion of the building where the explosion occurred. The theory is that it most have been deposited by someene who had gained access to the Admiralty °dim, and then walked through the corridors to the spot where the ex- plosion occurred. It to also thought, however, that an in- fernal machine has beeen delivered at the Admiralty ad- dressed to Lord Northbrcok, with the Intention of causing him serious injury. The design has been frustrated by hie absence from town. Soon after the explosion several tire engines erriyed, bat no oeCaSion was found for their employ- ruent, although eye witnesses state that a volume of smoke issued from the windows Contempo,aneously with the re- port of the explosion, Mr Gladstone sent over to make in- quiries shortly after the explosion occurred, and Mr Tre- velyan was amon2 the earliest visitors to arrive. After the examinatioo of Mr Swainson, Dr Dupre issued the follow- ing bulletin :—" Mr Swainson is suffering from severe con- cussion of the brain, but at present there are no alarming symptoms." Up to a late hour on Thursday evening the police au- thorities had not formed any theory as to the cause of the explosion. They' are inclined to the view that the explosive material may have been something other than dynamite, and contene that the position of the explosive argues a degree of deliberation on the part of the person who placed it there which would scarcely be expected from an indi- vidual who had made his way into the room with an infernal machine. and who had of course every incentive to leave again with all possible speed. After a careful interrogation of the d4ferent officials engaged about the building, the authorities have discarded the theory which was started that the explosion had been caused by a person employed at the Admiralty Offices. The notion to which they now lean is that a specimen of some missile boded with gun cotton had been submitted to the Admi- ralty authorities for examination, and that it had passed into Mr. Swainson's possession and had been placed by him for safe custody on the top of the book-case, where it explo- ded spontaneously. The story that the works of an Ameri- can clock had been found amongst the debris is explaiaed by the fact that a small timepiece usually kept in the room is missing, and is supposed to have been partially destroyed by the explosion. There doss not appear to be any corro- boration of the somewhat circumstantial narrative given to the reporters by a gentleman in the Paymaster-Getierare office in reference to two men, having the appearance of artisans, who were supposed to have obtained an eatry to the Admiralty by the private door of the First Lord's garden. The Central News understands "that there are strong reasons for believing that the explosive agent employed was neither dynamite nor any nitro conapund, but gunpowder. Mast of the characteristics which have hitherto marked dynamite explosions are missing. The damage done was alesurelly small, such as might have well been caused by the explosion in the book case of se few pounds of gun- powder." The Central News says :—Colonel Magendie and ether officials were busy throughout Friday at the Admiralty making inquiries and investigations in connection with the explosion. The debris in Mr Swainson's room has now been removed, and is being sifted in the rear of the build- ing. Sir VVilliain Harcourt paid another visit to the scene, and sabaequently had interviews with Colonel Magendie and Superintendent Williamson of Scotland-yard. No Special preparations of any importance have been taken by the Admiralty officials, as the building has long been well guarded, but the old waiting-room near the garden ha been temporarily closed. It has already been stated that the Admiralty Buildings sustained no structural damage, but it was discovered on Friday that the plaster on the other side of the sAid three feet thick party wall between Mr Swain- son's room, and the ante-room, was bulged out by the shock of the explosion. This, it is said, supports the theory that the explosive agent was gun-cottoa. The belief that the outrage was due te private malice gains ground. In view of the fact that the Assistant Seeretary has been the author of a scheme involving considerable reductions of the estab- lishment at the Admiralty, it is feared that he has been the victim of some act of vengeance, and more than one person connected with the department is said to be under police supervision. On inquiry at St Thomas's Hospital on Fri- day even'ag it was stated that Mr Swainson was progress- ing favourably.

One more point and I have done. Objection is made ilea whimsical way to our Sunday being "modelled upon the continential principle." I see nothiug very alarming in this. Certainly the workmen of the continent have considerably more "high days and holy days" than we have through the year, and if 'X. \V. was to see the people streaming off to the beer gardens on Sundays, he w mid be astonished ; to see the father and mother surrounded with their families seated under the dwarf trees, drinking their wine and listen- ing to the sweet strains of mnoic, is something not anite calculated to upset my nerves. In fact it is so alluring that a very large num,rr of Enelishmen hasten to avail them- selves of the pleasures derived therefrom. I understand that bands play in the public parks of London on Sundays. So they ought to do in the parks throughout the kingdom ; opee your libraries and museums Mr. Charles Marvin delivered a lecture on Russia the other-Sunday at Newcastle. Let us have similar intellectual treats here, and you will soon see drunkenness vanish, and moderation steadily increase. April 20, 1885. PETER PLYMLEY.

EVERTON V. HAVDOCK TEMPEBANCEL—This match Was played at Haydock on t:aturday, for the benefit of the Hay. dock Cottage Haqpital, and a pretty fair sum was realised, about 1,600 persons being present. Everton had the advan- tage of the wind during the first half, and Scored six goals to nil. In the second half the borne teain played up well, and, aided by the wind, scored twice, but the visitors added two more goals and won by eight to two. Everton were without Marriott, Dobson, and Pickering, and Whittle, who was hurt early in the second half of the game, kept goal, Lindsay taking his place forward. The goals were got by Farmer (three), Jefferson (two), Gibson (two), and (one).

I About two minutes later the Liverpool Cap holders again i rushed in front, and from a free kick Sans again scored i amid prolonged cheering. The subsequent play was of a true exciting character, as the home eleven continually I pressed the visitors and frequently shot for goal. No ad- ditional point was registered, however, and when time was called the Swifts were victorious by hhree goals to two. div.head: "BREACH OF PROMISE."
div.p: "BREACH OF PROMISE."

A SINGULAR CASE. At Warringtc,n County Court, on Thursday, a singular ease came on for hearing by his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The plaintiff; James Fellowes, a locksmith and bellhanger, was represented by Mr. A. Browne, and the defendant, a young woman named Miss Betsey Wrigley, who is a domestic servant at Widnes by Mr. 3.1, ore. Mr. Browne said that the claim was for £2 lBs, made under circumstances which he proceeded to detail. It seemed, be said, that plaintiff and defendant be- came engaged to each other in Nov. last, and court- ship went on for two or three mouths, at the end of which time it was arranged that they should be married. On the 24th January defenda-et requested her lover to buy her a dress to be married in. He con- sented, and they both went t a shop to buy one. Plaintiff paid £2 down, and the bill came to £1 4s 4d. The balance the defendant picked UP. That dress was simply paid for for the purpose of the defendant being married in it. Plaintiff also advanced his sweetheart 7s Gel as a loan, and paid for the dress , being made. On the 4th February, the day before the marriage should have taken place, the parties disagreed, and the wedding was put off. They afterwards again became engaged, but the match was now broken off altogether, and his client sued for the amount he had paid for the dress and had advanced to defendant.—His Honour : That was paid in consideration of her engaging herself to be he married to him ?—Mr. Browne : Yes.—His Hon- our : Titen you are trying an action for breach of promise under the guise of getting this money back —Mr. Browne : Plaintiff is a man, and it is not his fault that the match was broken off.—His Honour : That does not signify. The dress was got in consideration of the malriage.—Mr. Browne : And that marriage has not taken place through her fault.—His Honour said that if he tried the case he should have to go into the question of breach of promise of marriage. The money was paid as a gift upon a good consideration at the time. Bubsequently the defendant broke the contract, and should be sued for breach of that contract. It was an indirect way of trying to bring before the court an action for breach of promise, which he could not entertain, Mr. Moore : Then there will be a verdict for the defendant with costs —His Honour There will be a non•suit.

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.
At a meeting of the Rail way Association on: Priday it was detertniued to abandon the nine railway bills now before Parliament.

NATIONAL LAND COMPANY.—Lord Carnarvon presided on Friday at Willis's Rooms, London, over a very large and inflnential meeting convened for the purpose of establishing a National Land Company to buy land in largo quantities, and to sell it in small lots on easy terms of purchase. Resolutions in support of the scheme and appointing a pro- visional committee were passed.

div.head: TdREEt PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH IN LONDON.
div.p: TdREEt PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH IN LONDON.

Shortly after two o'clock on Friday morning a fire broke out in an oilshop in Union-street, Borough, London, and raged with great rapidity, some petroleum which exploded adding to the terror of the scene. The occupants of the house rushed to the windows in their nightdresses cryiing for help, and great excitement followed. A little girl five yeArs old was thrown out of the window by. an elder sister, and caaght by the crowd beneath, as was also her sister, aged four ; but as the third child, age l three was being thrown out it struck against a projecting signboard, and was. 30 severely injured that it had to be taken to the hospital. The elder sister herself, who had saved the others, then leaped from the window, but was so terribly hurkthat she is not expected to recover. After the fire had been sub- dued k was found that the proprietor of the shop, his wife, and young son bad been burnt to death, THE PRINCE OF WALES AT BELFAST.

It was raining hard at eleven o'clock on Friday morning when the Prince and Princess of Wales quitted the Royal yacht Osborne, in Carrickfer,zus Roads, and steamed to Belfast in the steamer Manx Q awn, and there was every indication of a very wet day. This,.however. did not deter a great crowd assembling in the vicinity of Donegal Quay, where the first ceremonial of the day took place. Ihe Manx Queen steamed up alongside the quay shortly after twelve o'clock, where a body of the Harbour Commissioners was assembled, and they presented an address congratulating the Prince on his visit to the prosperous and thriving capital of Ulster, accompanied by the Princess. His Royal High- , ness took his stand on a raised platform in the shed on the quay, the crowds in the streets near by and the company surrounding the platform cheering meanwhile, and suitably , replied. The Prince afterwards declared the quay open, and visited several of the principal manufactories in the town.

SUAKTM, FarrAY —General •Graham, accompanied by his staff, left at six o'clock this morning by train for Han- doub, whEnce they will ride to Tambouk. The railway is now laid for a distance of three miles beyond Handoub, and its construction is still being continued.

div.head: 'HE WAR CRISIS.
div.p: 'HE WAR CRISIS.

The Berlin correspondent of the Gau/ois telegraphs that the Emperor has declared—" So long as I live, peace shall Rot be broken." Oa the other hand, a well-informed French official, connected with the corps diploatatipze, says that Russia is determined to go to war rather than retreat from the position she has taken. A telegraph wire has again been broken between Meshed and Teheran and Sir Peter Lumsden. Direct communica- tion with this country is once more cut eff.

It is stated that Colonel Nicholson is not to go to Herat to report upon the defences there, as the Ameer is unable to ensure his safety. An advertisement is published in some London newspapers in the Polish language calling upon the Poles to wait patiently until a good opportunity arrives, when they may strike a blow for freedom. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE PEACE

div.head: SOCIETY.
div.p: SOCIETY.

Replying on Friday to a memorial in favour of peace, forwarded by the Liverpool Peace Society, Mr Gladstone says :—The memorialists may rest assured that no efforts will be spared by Her Majesty's Government t) secure by pacific means an honourable settlement of the points at is- sue with Russia as regards the northern frontier of Afghanistan. THE CZAR AND THE PENJDEH INCIDENT.

The "St. Petersburger Ziltung" states that the Emperor has sent a large number of Crosses of St. George to General Komaroff for distribution amongst those soldiers who showed the greatest bravery in the fight on the Kushk river ; and also that the Commander-in-Chief has been requested to send in the names of officers who distinguished themselves on that occasion. It is hoped, adds the writer, that General Komaroff will also receive the much coveted de- coration.

ST. PFrrysnstiumn, FRIDAY —An order of; the Minister of Marine, dated the 18th met, directs that the list of naval officerS available for active service shall inciude the generals on half-pay specially attached to the Naval Department. It has also been ordered that all admirals, staff officer% or superior officers on the active or half-pay list having at- tained a-certain age shag be pensioned off unless they join the Naval Reserve. The ociel Messenger this morning Publishes a list of officers who have been pensioned cif in accordant:in with this order.

div.head: ENGLISH WAR PREPARATIONS.
div.p: ENGLISH WAR PREPARATIONS.
In response to the recent Admiralty circular a consider- able number of naval pensioners in the Nore district ha..-e voluateered for active service.

The corvette Pylades, under orders for active service, brought her machinery trials to a satisfactory conclusion at Sheerness on Friday, and extra hands are now being em- ployed on her to complete her for sea. Considerable inconvenience having been caused at the Admiralty by the large attendance of owners of tag boats and small cargo steamers anxious to secure charter, Mr Bangham, assistant director of transports, has notified that be cannot give interviews to gentlemen on chartering business.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Hausa met at 4 o'clock. TRH DRCLARATFON OF PARIS.—Lord LYMINOTON, in consequence of the preeent unsatisfactory relations with , Russia, gave notice to draw attention to the Declaration of 'Paris of 1858,and to move that it was our duty to with- draw from that Declaration, and thus maintain ancient mari- time rights essential to the power and prosperity of our Em- pire. Mescsmetersotrs.—The Scot,* Burgh and Police Bill framed to consolidate and amend the municipal legislation of Scotch Burghs wes read a second time. The report of amendments on the Infants' Bill was considered. Sub- section 2, claw* 3, givlag a wife predeceasing her husband, power to appoint two guardians for her children, was op- posed by the Margais of Salisbury on the ground that courts of law called on to revise appointments had no defi- nite principle to guide them. The House divided, and the clause was retained without amendment by 42 against 28 votes. The Irish Solicitors' Bill passed the third reading, and the Egyptian Loan Bill passed through committee without discussion. The House adjourned at seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. THE WAR CRISIS. Mr. McCo.ix gave notice that on an early day be would call attention to the declaration of Paris and, move a reso- lution.-'-Lord FITZMAURICH, replying to Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, declined to say whether the despatch published in the papers from M. de Giers, purporting to be the answer of the Russian Government to our Government was authen- tic —Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. Richards, Slid, in the correspondence that had taken place with Russia, they had never said anything to the prejudice of arbitration. Re- plying to Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, he said the Government had no information as to the reperted march el the Rus- sians on Herat.—Lord Emmet:arcs said no new informs. tion had been received that day from General Lumsden. latsit REOISTRATION.—The House then went into Corn- reittre on the Registration of Voters (Ireland) Bill.—Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN proposed an amendment to the second clause with ths view of giving effect to the decisien of the Cerninittee on the English Bill, and that the forms for bringing upon the register the persons entitled to vote should be embodied in a schedule, instead of being fixed by order in Council.—Mr. GIBSON asked for time to con- sider the schedule, and Mr. Campbell Binnerman assen- ted.—Mr. PARNELL accused the Government of negligence in pressing the Itiah Bill forward, and said they had thus afforded an excuse to r.he front Opposition bench for del eying is progress.—The. amendment and clause were agreed to.—Mr GIBSON moved the omission of the third clause, the object of which was to E et out that receivieg dispensary medical relief should not be a ground for dis- qualifyiug voters. He insisted that the passiog of such a clause would be to demoralise the status of the voter.—Mr SExTON did not see that the reception of temporary medical help in any way would interfere with the independence of the status of the voter. He could not see why the voter who could not afford to pay his doctor should be shut Oct from exorcising his vote. The object of the amendment was clearly an:attempt to defeat the operation of the Fran. chine Bill in Ireland.—A long discussion ensued, during which Mr rPO'Colneon said hostility to the clause was rot to preserve the Mato of the IrlshMsn, bat to deprive ,

him of all voice in the destinies of his own country.—Mr CAMPBELL-BANNEEMAN defended the clause, and insisted that the proposal to omit it was a round about way of dis- franchising voters in Ireland.—The clause was finally agreed to by 76 to 20 votes.—Clause 3 was agreed to, as were clauses 4 and 5. On clause 6, which provided for the remunerating of officers for carrying into effect the Regis- tration Acts, being proposed, considerable discussion en- sued.
