A CANAL MYSTERY. On Tmsday afternoon the body of a man, then unknown, horribly mutilated, was dragged out of the Bridgwater canal near Pickering's Bridge, Thelwall, near Warrington, by men in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation Companyethe captain of a passing steam tug having stated that his boat i had "caught some.hing." The body was removed to the Pickering Arms, Thelwall, and information at once given to the police. Sergeant Harrington ( Lymm) instituted in- ! quiries that resulted in the identification of the deceased— whose body was cut in such a manner as to at first suggest that a murder had been committed and the victim then thrown into the water—and yesterday Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner, and a jury, i rquired into the circumstances of the death at the inn where the body had been deposited.— I Charlotte Bradbury, of 7, Essex-street, off Tamworth-street, Hulme, Manchester, was the first witness called. She said that she had identified the body of the deceased as that of her husband, who had been a salesman in the employ of Messrs Edmondson, smallware dealers, Shudeleill, Manches- ter. He was 68 years old. She last saw him alive on Easter Monday., the 6th mat, at about six o'clock in the evening. At that hoar she left home, and on returning at seven o'clock, was informed that her husband had gone for a walk. She never again saw him alive. They had been married seven years. Deceased attended regularly to his work, was strong and healthy, was not subject to fits, and was of sober habits. He was comfortably off, had no trouble on his mind, and she did not think that he had an enemy in the world. She made all possible inquiries to learn his whereabouts, but failed. —Jessie Craik Parry, who had for six months lodged with the deceased, acid thet when he left th house on Easter Monday evening he remarked "I think I shall go out for a bit of a walk." He was not in the habit of walking by the canal, and she knew of no reason that he should do so on that occasion.—William Bowers, benksman in the employ of the Bridgewater Navigation ' Company, who lives at Thelwall boat-home, deposed that when at work near Pickering's Bridge a tug boat passed, and Captaia William Blower, who was in charge, said " I have caught something, but I do not know what; it is ether a man or a woman," Afterwards the ctnal was dragged, and tlee body of deceazed taken out.—Dr. Thomas Gellimore (Lymm) stated the result of a post mortem ex- amination made on Wednesday. The body appeared to have been in the water about three weeks. There was a lacerated wound about four inches long along the left jaw, and one about eight inches long separating the muscles ant superficial structures of the neck and the chest. On the left side of the chest was a lacerated wound about eight inches long, the left arm was divided about the middle by a lacerated wound, so that the arm only hung by a slip; on the right shoulder were four parallel lacerated wounds as though caused by a rake; on the upper part of the left thigh at the right side were two superficial incised wounds about an inch long, and there was a lacerated wound about about two inches long en the left thigh. Other injuries were : Superficial skin wound, about four inches long, on the left shin bone, a deep lacer- ated wound, about three inches long, on the right thigh, two or three parallel superficial wounds on the right leg, two bones of the right forearm fractured, a contusion, about twelve inches long and three broad, extending from the left shoulder to the midefle of the back, a large irregulur con- tusion over the right shoulder, about four inches long by five broad, left colltr bone and ribs fractured downwards, left shoulder blade fractured, right shoulder blade and ribs fractured, ribs and front of Chest en both sides fractured, On opening the chest he fund a lacerated wound about two inches long on the right side of the heart. The lungs presented nothing indicative of death by drowning. On taking out the lungs he saw that the spine was fractured. There was also a lacerated wound on the liver, the internal wounds corresponding with the external. The upper part of the head, including scelp, bones and brains, was missing, and the remaining bones were broken into small pieces. The left upper jaw bone was broken and the teeth of that j tw were missing, as well as the molars of the lower jaw. He was of opinion that all the wounds, contusions, and fractures, were caused after death. There was an absence of signs of death from drowning, and he was unable to definitely form an opinion as to the Cillse Of death. It was possible that it had been through drowning, but he had rather not give a definite opinion, as so many signs were wanting.—Mrs Bradbury, recalled, said that semetimes her husband went to Pomona, and is doing so would probably go near the canal.—This was all the evidence, and a conversation followed concerning the injuries that might be inflicted by the fans of a steamer on a body in the water.—The Coroner remarked that the fact that none of the wounds had, in the opinion of the doctor, been caused during life, removed a deal of sus- picion, and the jury, after a few moments' consultation, re- turned a verdict of " Found Drowned."

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

, THE FEvatt HOSPITAL—On Tuesday the members of the Sanitary Committee of Bootle, accompanied by their medical officer and borough surveyor, paid a visit to the Warring- ton Fever Hospital, and, as is usual with visitors to this establishment-, they were well pleased with the arrangements and the way in which thehospital is maniged by Dr Gornall. WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. —On Sunday evening the Rev .1 Yonge preached another of his monthly sermons to young men in the above churn +, in the presence of a large congregation. His text was Judges viii., 20, " And he (Gideon) said unto Jether, his first-born, up and ' slay them ; but the youth drew not his sword for he feared, because he was yet a youth." Emu oeuat CHURCH BAND OF HOPE.—On Monday even- ing a concert was given by members of this Band of Hope, when the Rev W Mules occupied the chair. Messrs H Gandy and W Parsons gave readings, and Miss Ray gave a song. Dialogues were given by Mr Teare, Miss Ada Jack- son,. Messrs H and F Garnett, and recitations by the Misses Louie and Lizzie Hobin and Clara Lloyd, and Messrs W and J Jackson, THE WELLINGTON FOOTBALL CHALLENGE CUP. On Monday evening, a meeting to receive entrance fees, was held at the committee rooms of the Earlestown Football Club, E4riestown. There was a fair attendance, and Mr Blair presideel. During the evening entrance fees were re- ceived from the following clubs :—Warrington Association, St Helen's St Mark, Haydock St James's (two teams), Eariestown Rovers, Ashton Recreation, Sankey Refiners, Stubshaw Cross (Ashton) Wanderers, and Virargrave. It is expected other teams will enter the contest before next Mon- day night, when the ties in the first round of the competi- tion will be drawn.

Lecruams ON PlTREltoLogs.—On Monday and Tuesday the Rev J J Brown (Australia) delivered lectures on pbrim- oloeical subjects, in 8011-street new schools, before coed audiences. On the first-named evening the chair was occu- pied by Mr E J Guest, and Dr Mackie presided on Tuesday. The first lecture was on "Heads and faces," and proved an interesting one, Mr Brown dealing with the subject in a pleas int manner. At the close several of the audience were phrenologically examined by Mr Brown. " Mistaken No- tions " was the subject of the second lecture, and Mr Brown gave his audience some sound advice on every-day matters. Afterwards he was thanked for his services, which were given gratuitously in aid of the S:lver-street school brass band.

CONCERT' BY TEN YEVa.E MIIISTRELS —On Saturday evening the Yevrah (Harvey) Minstrels, of Liverpool, gave a concert at the Public Hall, Rylands-street, in aid of the building fund of the new schools, Latchford. There wa• a large audience, and the programme, which was princia pally composed of tha comic element, was well rendered and much enjaved. The minstrel songs were excellently well given, and the jokes on the whole were good. Signor Electro interested the audience by sketching portraits in chalk with marvellous rapidity, and drew the likeness of the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) very truthfully. He also drew sketches of General Gordon, Sir Garnet Wolseley, and ethers who have made their names famous, amidst the ap- plausd of the audience. Professor •` Bloquehead" gave an amusing lecture, and "Rum'ns from Rome, or Ajax and Hercuks," concluded a very good entertainment.

„ Tirt MATfiON OF THE HOSPITAL.--.Mrs Jones, who has for the last two years filled in the most efficient and satisfac- , tory manner theresponsible office of matron of the Warring- ton Infectious Diseases- Hospital, has received the appoint- ment of matron and superintendent of nursing of the Royal United Hospital, Bath. The Sanitary Committee, presided over by Alderman Burgess, at their meeting on Wednesday, in accepting Mrs Jones's resignation, passed the following resolhtion :—” Resolved. that the resignation of Mrs Ida J Jones, the matron of the Infectious Diseases Hospital, be ac- cepted, she baying obtained the appointment of matron and superintendent of nursing of the Royal United Hospital, Bath. The committee, in accepting the resignation, record their entire satisfaction with the way in which Mrs Jones. hAs discharged her duties since her appointment in August, 1853."

DROWNING, FATALITY.—Richard Arthur Johnson, four years of age, son 0 Stephen Johns:on, herbalist, 46, Napiel. street, was on Satnrday drowned in a brook of mud and water whilst playing in the vicinity of Lord Nelson-street. On Monday, Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, held atbin- quiry into the occurr,mce at the Bridewell, when a man named Edwin Brown, 21, Lord Nelson-street, said that on Saturday afternoon he was standhg at the back door of his house, when a little boy told him that some one ha ia fallen into the brook. He went there and found deceasoil quite dead, in ab mt 15 inches of water. There was nothing to prevent a person walking into the brook. The waste land at the back did not belong to, the houses.—The Coroner : The pecole living la the hcr.sea have no legal right to go on the ground? No; but there is a public highway neat the chemical works—Thu Coroner said that as far as he could ascertain persona would have to walk off the footpath to .let into danger, and on to the land that was not pub- lic. It was open for the jury to make any presentment they thought fit for the future preservation of life, but it al)- pearid to him that only trespassers eould get into danger. —A juryman remarked that the land surrounding the brook was a playground, for the children of the neighbourhood, and that it was a wonder more children had not been drowned —The jury Nit:mfd verdict of " Accidental death,"

THE QUEEN. Aix LES-PAINS, MONDAY.—This morning the Queen and Princes Beatrice, attended by Lady Churchill, walked and afterwards drove out; and in the afternoon her Majesty and the Priucess went for a drive. The Queen will leave for Darmstadt on Wednesday at three o'clock. Aix-LES-PAINS, WEDNESDAY.—The Queen and Princess Beatrice drove out this morning. Her Majesty, accompanied by the Princess Beatrice and attended by the Royal suite, left Aix-les-Bains at three o'clock this afternoon, the local authorities, who had been invited, being present at the sta- tion. The journey to Darmstadt will be broken at Fribnrg for dinner. DemersrADT, WEDNEsDLy.—Her Majesty the Queen is expected to arrive here LT-morrow morning at eight o'clock. DARMST4DT, THORSDAy.—The Queen and Princess Beat- rice, acconbanied by their suite, arrived here at ten minutes peat eight this morning, and were received at the station by the members of the Grand Ducal Family. FRANCE AND THE SUPPRESSION OF TES "BO& PHORB EGYPTIFN." CAIRO, MONDAy.—Nubar Pasha has replied to the French demands in reference to the recent suppression of the Bos- phore Egyptien, that the Capitulations hiving been agreed to by the Porte, he cannot give a definite answer until after consultation with the Ottoman Government in regard to its interpretation of the Capitulations and the form to be given to the reply of the Egyptian Government.--LATER.— The French Government has intimated to Nubar Pasha its willingness to grant him time in order to consult with the Porte on the subject of suppression of the Bosphoec Egyptien. CAIRO, I'lmm:we—The French diplomatic agent this morning intimated to Nubar Pasha that the French Foreign Miaister was not satisfied with the reply made to the French demand fer reparation on accouet of the Bosphore Egyptien. The French representative added that he was instructed to give the Egyptian Government until four o'clock this afternoon to reply. Nubar Pasha informed him that the Porte approved of the action of the Egyptian Gov- ernment. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—A telegram from London to the Temps expresses the belief that the affair of the Bosphore Egypt lea will be settled without much delay. THE SUEZ CANAL. • PARIS, MONDAY.—The International Commission to-day, after hearing the views of MM. Ferdinand and Charles de Lesseps, finally agreed to the elauses relating to the neu- trality of the Sweet-water Canal The object of the clauses is to prevent the possibility of 'sum lia and Port Said being deprived of water, and the working of the canal being thereby stopped. The work of the Commission is proceeding very slowly. FRENCH TROOPS IN THE SUEZ CANAL. A French transport arrived in the Suez Canal on Wed- nesday morning. Other two French ships, with nearly 2.000 men on board, stayed nearly a week in the Canal. They were, however, followed and closely watched by the British ironclad Invincible, whose sealed orders from Alexandria, it is believed. Included instructions to prevent any landing of French troops in the Canal. FRANCE AND CHINA. PARIS, Satrunnair.—From General Briere de Lisle "On the 16th inst. some Chinese, with a flag of truce, pre- sented themselves at the outposts at Kip to assure me that my letters had been sent to the Commander-in-Chief at Langson. The same eeening our emissaries reported that the Chinese were retiring towards the north."—lt is semi- officially stated this afternoon that the recent engagement at Kee was due solely to the difficulty of comtntenicetien having prevented the Chinese -commauders from receiving the order to cease hostilities. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—The Minister of War has received the following telegram from General Briere de l'lsle : Hanoi, Tuesday.—My letters have reached the Chinese officers on the Red River, and hostilities with the Chinese army are now everywhere suspended. Yesterday a Chinese officer from Langson came to Kep with a flag of truce. THE RISING IN CANADA. OTTAWA, MONDAY.—The Indians on the Morlyville Re- serve, in the North-West Territory, have sent to-day to the Dominion Government, through the Chiefs Bear Paw, Big Stoney, and Chiniguy, renewed assurances of their fealty to the British Crown, saying that they rely on British justice as represented by the Canadian Govern- ment. OTTAWA, SIINDAY.-1141f of General Middleton's force will cross the Saskatchewan River at Clarke's Crossing, the other half going down the east b.nk towards Batoches. Three of Riel's scouts have been captured. They belong to the Jeeton Sioux Indians, and state that their tribes are tin. witting allies of Riel. General Middleton released one of the scouts, telling him to go back to his peopleeand say that Canada was not at war with the good Indians who are willing to go to the Reserves, Riel has issued a manifesto, statingthat in 1876, 1877, and 1878 the half-breeds made urgent representations to the Government officials without effect. He blames the surveyors for cutting up their land, and the inspectors for taking away their wood and water rights, and affirms that he did not fire the first shot, and , that he is being hunted to death. Rail's followers, however, are deserting. Intelligence from Battleford and Prince Albert states all well there. The flying column from Swift Current is making good progress towards Battle- ford. The Celgarey force will leave for Edmonton on Mon- day next. Orraws, TIJESDAY.—News received here to-day an- I nonnoes that some messengers sent to Battleford report that Fort Pitt has fallen. Two policemen had been killed, and it was feared that the wools party had been massacred. A number of Indians are stated to be going down the river towards Battleford. The flying column is pushing on to its , relief. Orrawa, TurresDay.—Mr J Dickens, with the police from Fort Pitt, has arrived at Battleford. He reports that only one man was killed at Fort Pitt, and that the settlers I have gone to the Indian camps. The relief flying column will reach Battleford at noon to-morrow. MACK ON A SPANISH WEST AFRICAN SETTLEMENT. MADRID, WEDNESDAY.--Aceording to intelligence re- ceived here from the Canary Islands, tome native tribes recently made an attack upon the Spanish settlement at Cape Blanco, on the West Coast of Africa. The settlers were consequently obliged to take refuge en a Spanish gunboat. The reports of the occurrence are somewhat vague, and farther details are awaited. HUNGARY. REFORM OF THE UPER HOUSE. 1 PESTH, WEDNESDAY.—The Lower House of the Hun- garian Diet, after several days' debate, has passed, by 219 against 133 votes, the bill for the reform of the Upper ! House in the terms agreed upon by that assembly.
